**Audience**: an engineer who has already scraped a CSV of reviews / tickets and fitted a scikit-learn classifier — and wants to know *why* BM25 beats TF-IDF, or why a BERT fine-tune blows up the vocab. **Empirical first**: F1 dropping after aggressive stemming; a tokenizer that multiplies FR tokens vs EN — then we name BoW, embeddings, transformers.

From tokenization to industrial text mining (TF-IDF/BM25, embeddings, topics, NER, fine-tuning). Mandatory P2 foundation for the M2 module [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Build a complete text processing pipeline, from raw corpus to usable features.
-   Represent documents with bag of words, TF-IDF and BM25, build a search engine on these foundations (inverted index) and evaluate its rankings (MAP, nDCG).
-   Train and interpret word embeddings.
-   Infer latent topics in a corpus with topic models.
-   Classify texts, from Naive Bayes to transformer fine-tuning.
-   Label sequences (named entity recognition) with HMMs and CRFs.
-   Fine-tune a transformer for a given NLP task.
-   Build content-based and collaborative recommenders (matrix factorization), and use text features for click prediction and social media monitoring.
-   Conduct a text mining project in an industrial context, from data to production deployment.

### Course outline

-   **Review: vector spaces and probabilities** — the two lenses of the course: representing a document as a vector, reasoning in terms of laws and likelihood.
-   **The text processing pipeline** — segmentation, cleaning, normalization: the decisive craft before any model.
-   **Bag of words, TF-IDF and BM25** — the classical representations, the scoring function that powers information retrieval, the inverted index and ranking metrics.
-   **Text classification** — from Naive Bayes to neural models: the reference task of NLP.
-   **Word embeddings** — moving from counting to prediction: word vectors that carry meaning.
-   **Topic models** — discovering the latent topics of a corpus, with EM as the engine.
-   **Sequences: NER, HMM, CRF** — labeling named entities with structured sequential models.
-   **Transformers for NLP** — attention, fine-tuning, and the shift toward large pretrained models.
-   **Industrial text mining** — summaries, keywords, deduplication, a ticket case study, recommendation systems, web advertising and social media analysis; volumes, annotation budgets, deployment and monitoring.
-   **Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Buscaldi)** — a tour of the research work of Vazirgiannis and Buscaldi (self-study).
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Work through the review section: dot products and conditional probabilities are used explicitly in every subsequent chapter.
-   Once, build a bag of words and a TF-IDF score yourself on a mini-corpus: everything that follows is understood by contrast with this baseline.
-   Before each model, write down on paper what it assumes (independence, word order, latency): this is what enables practical choices.
-   Hand-label a few sentences for a NER task: you will measure the cost of annotation, the central constraint of industrial NLP.
-   Read the transformers chapter in parallel with the attention chapter of your Deep Learning course ([P1, ch. 6](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch6), or [P2, text generation with transformers](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-textgen)): the two reinforce each other.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; they prepare the graded assignments and the bridge to the LLMs module.

## 0. Review: vector spaces and probabilities {#ch0}

This course reads text through two lenses: as vectors (a document is a point, similarity is an angle) and as random sequences (a document is drawn from a distribution, and learning means maximizing a likelihood). The review below recalls the tools of both lenses and points to the chapter where each one is used.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 background used
:::

-   **Vector spaces**: basis, dimension, projection; cosine similarity
    $$
    \cos(u, v) = \frac{u^\top v}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}
    $$
    — invariant under dilation ($\cos(u,v)=\cos(\lambda u, v)$ for $\lambda > 0$, which "cancels out" document lengths); the $\ell_2$ norm will be used to normalize TF-IDF vectors;
-   **Linear algebra**: singular value decomposition
    $$
    \mathbf{X} \approx \mathbf{U}_k \Sigma_k \mathbf{V}_k^\top
    $$
    — the engine of LSA (ch. 5) and the direct cousin of PCA (Machine Learning module);
-   **Conditional probabilities and Bayes**:
    $$
    \mathbb{P}(c \mid d) \propto \mathbb{P}(d \mid c)\,\mathbb{P}(c)
    $$
    — the Naive Bayes classifier (ch. 3) follows directly from it; the Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$, conjugate of the multinomial — the foundation of LDA (ch. 5, where a box defines it);
-   **Markov chains and dynamic programming** ([Reinforcement Learning ch. 0](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch0), session 1 of that course): forward/backward and Viterbi (ch. 6) are Bellman recursions on a chain; the collapsed Gibbs sampler (ch. 5) is a chain on topic assignments; the TextRank (ch. 8) is a Markov chain raised to a power;
-   **Likelihood, MLE and EM**: word2vec (ch. 4), LDA (ch. 5), Naive Bayes (ch. 3) and the Unigram tokenizer (ch. 1) are all likelihood maximizations — by SGD, Gibbs, direct counting or EM;
-   **Entropy and perplexity**: for a language model,
    $$
    \mathrm{PPL} = \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{t} \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\big)
    $$
    — the universal quality measure of a generative model of text (M2 LLMs, ch. 3).
::::

::: note
[How to read this course]{.tag} Each chapter follows the same triptych:

1.  a *representation* of text (counts, weights, vectors, distributions, latent topics);
2.  a learning *algorithm* with its statistical justification;
3.  a quantified *evaluation*.

The [thm]{.tag}/prop boxes contain the proven results; the proofs come at the end of each box. References of the form "module X, chapter N" point to the other courses of the master's program.

The natural extension of this module is the M2 "Large Language Models" course, which picks up tokenization (ch. 1), BM25 (ch. 2), sentence embeddings (ch. 7) and transformers where we leave them.
:::

## 1. The text processing pipeline {#ch1}

Concrete scene: 50,000 support tickets in French and English. A first pipeline lowercases the text, splits it into "words" with a regular expression and feeds TF-IDF features to a logistic regression: macro-F1 0.62. Without NFKC normalization, two encodings of "café" count as two different types; with aggressive stemming, "connection" and "connector" merge and the macro-F1 drops to 0.51. This chapter fixes the pipeline *before* the model.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Inconsistent train/prod tokenizer (ghost vocab); normalizing too late (Unicode duplicates); judging a classifier on overall accuracy when 3 classes dominate. All three sabotage an LLM fine-tune as much as a toy BoW.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Standard pipeline]{.tag} **Raw text** → cleaning (HTML, case, accents, Unicode) → sentence segmentation → **tokenization** (splitting into units: words, subwords, characters) → lexical normalization (*stemming* raw root / *lemmatization* canonical form; stopwords) → representation (ch. 2, 4, 5) → model (ch. 3, 6, 7) → evaluation. Each stage destroys information; the engineer's craft is deciding *which* information is expendable for the task at hand.
:::

### 1.1. Unicode normalization and "clean" text

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Unicode normal forms]{.tag} The same glyph admits several encodings: "é" = one codepoint `U+00E9` in **NFC** (canonical composition), but two (`e` + combining accent `U+0301`) in **NFD**. **NFKC** goes further: ligature "ﬁ" → "fi", digit "²" → "2", full-width letters → ASCII. Two strings that are visually identical but distinct in bytes break counting, deduplication and search; so we normalize *before anything else* (in practice NFKC, or NFC if typography and units must be preserved).
:::

-   **Case**: `lower()` merges "Polytechnique" and "polytechnique" but also the acronym and the common word; in French, *keep the accents* in lowercase ("élève" ≠ "eleve");
-   **Sentence segmentation**: rules (punctuation + capital letter) or learning (Punkt, Kiss & Strunk 2006); real pitfalls: "M.", "etc.", German abbreviations ("z. B."), period before a closing quote. Bad segmentation wrecks ch. 8 (extractive summarization: the sentence is the unit being selected);
-   **Stemming vs lemmatization**: the stemmer (Porter, Snowball) cuts off suffixes by rules — fast, crude, suited to information retrieval; the lemmatizer uses a dictionary and morphology ("sont" → "être") — slower, better for fine-grained analysis. In industry: stemmer for search, lemmatizer for analysis.

### 1.2. Subword tokenization: BPE, WordPiece, Unigram, SentencePiece

::: note
[Why subwords]{.tag} Splitting on spaces works poorly: German compounds ("Donaudampfschifffahrt"), French elisions ("l'arbre": 1 or 2 tokens?), some Asian languages write without spaces, and any closed vocabulary runs into unknown words (typos, neologisms, product references). **Subword tokenizers** learn, on the corpus, a fixed-size vocabulary (\~32k-128k) whose concatenation reconstructs *any* string: frequent words = 1 token, rare words = a sequence of pieces.
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 1.3 — BPE (Byte Pair Encoding, Sennrich et al. 2016)]{.tag} Initial vocabulary: characters (or bytes). Iteratively: (1) count all pairs of adjacent symbols in the corpus (weighted by word frequencies); (2) merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol; (3) repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size $|V|$. The result is an ordered set of *merge rules*; tokenizing a new text = applying the merges in the learned order.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — Step-by-step BPE training]{.tag} Mini-corpus (words, frequencies): `base`×5, `bases`×4, `basse`×3, `basique`×2. Initial alphabet: b, a, s, e, i, q, u. We write each word as a sequence of symbols and count adjacent pairs:

  Step   Most frequent pairs                                                         Chosen merge
  ------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------
  1      (b,a)=14, (a,s)=14, (s,e)=12, (e,s)=4, (s,s)=3, (s,i)=(i,q)=(q,u)=(u,e)=2   **ba** (14; tie with (a,s), arbitrary choice)
  2      (ba,s)=14, (s,e)=12, (e,s)=4, (s,s)=3, …                                    **bas** (14)
  3      (bas,e)=9, (e,s)=4, (bas,s)=3, (s,e)=3, …                                   **base** (9)
  4      (base,s)=4, (bas,s)=3, (s,e)=3, …                                           **bases** (4)
  5      (bas,s)=3, (s,e)=3, …                                                       **bass** (3)
  6      (bass,e)=3, …                                                               **basse** (3)

After these six merges, `base`, `bases` and `basse` are whole tokens, while `basique` is still `bas`+`i`+`q`+`u`+`e` (four more merges would make it whole); an unexpected word like "basiste" breaks down into a known prefix (`bas`, or `basi` once more merges are learned) followed by single characters: never an unknown token, at worst a longer sequence. *This is exactly the mechanism, pushed to bytes and 128k tokens, that equips GPT and Llama — developed in M2 LLMs, ch. 1.*
:::

::: thm
[Variants 1.5 — WordPiece (BERT), Unigram (T5), SentencePiece]{.tag}

-   **WordPiece**: the same merge loop, but a pair's score is $\frac{f(x,y)}{f(x)\,f(y)}$ — we merge the pair whose *relative* frequency increases the most, a proxy for the likelihood gain of a unigram model (justification: merging $x,y$ replaces two symbols with one; the gain in bits is all the greater as the collocation is over-represented relative to independence);
-   **Unigram** (Kudo, 2018): a *generative* model — a candidate vocabulary (characters + frequent substrings), each segment $s$ has a probability $p(s)$, a word is segmented by Viterbi by maximizing $\sum_j \log p(s_j)$.

    Training by EM: **E** — for each word, the posterior distribution over its segmentations (∝ product of the $p(s_j)$, computable by a forward dynamic program); **M** — $p(s)$ = normalized expected counts; then *pruning* of the segments that degrade the likelihood the least, until the target size $|V|$.

    Unlike BPE, the segmentation is probabilistic and admits several analyses (subword regularization);
-   **SentencePiece**: a *language-independent* layer that treats the sentence as a sequence of bytes, the space becoming a "▁" symbol; no pre-tokenization on spaces — essential for languages without spaces and for multilingual settings (it is the foundation of Llama and T5).
:::

```python
import re
from collections import Counter

# --- Toy BPE: learning merges on the mini-corpus of example 1.4 ---
words = {"b a s e": 5, "b a s e s": 4, "b a s s e": 3, "b a s i q u e": 2}
merges = []
for _ in range(8):
    pairs = Counter()
    for w, f in words.items():
        sym = w.split()
        for pair in zip(sym, sym[1:]):
            pairs[pair] += f
    if not pairs:
        break
    best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get)          # most frequent adjacent pair
    merges.append(best)
    big = " ".join(best)
    words = {re.sub(r"(?<!\S)" + re.escape(big) + r"(?!\S)", "".join(best), w): f
             for w, f in words.items()}
print("merges:", merges[:6])
# tokenize a new word = replay the merges in the learned order
def encode(word, merges):
    sym = list(word)
    for a, b in merges:
        i, out = 0, []
        while i < len(sym):
            if i + 1 < len(sym) and (sym[i], sym[i+1]) == (a, b):
                out.append(a + b); i += 2
            else:
                out.append(sym[i]); i += 1
        sym = out
    return sym
print(encode("basiste", merges))
```

### 1.3. Stopwords, n-grams, collocations

-   **Stopwords**: to be removed for classical text mining (they saturate the BoW); to be *kept* for transformers — negation ("ne…pas") and syntax matter. The decision must be justified by the task, not by habit;
-   **N-grams**: sequences of $n$ tokens; "New York" (bigram) ≠ "New" + "York"; in classification, moving from unigrams to bigrams captures compositional polarity ("pas cher"); cost: the vocabulary explodes (potentially $|V|^n$) — hence `ngram_range=(1,2)` and `min_df` in the code of ch. 3;
-   **Collocations**: bigrams whose frequency exceeds what independence predicts, measured by mutual information $\mathrm{PMI}(x,y) = \log \frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)P(y)}$ — a criterion reused as-is in ch. 2 to justify IDF, and in ch. 5 for topic coherence.

## 2. Bag of words, TF-IDF and BM25 {#ch2}

Most models cannot read strings: they need vectors. This chapter turns each document into a vector of word counts, reweights the counts so that informative words dominate (TF-IDF), and derives BM25, the scoring function that still powers search engines.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Bag of words (BoW)]{.tag} A document = a vector of counts over the vocabulary $V$ (order lost): $d \in \mathbb{N}^{|V|}$. Documents × terms matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{N}^{n \times |V|}$ — *extremely sparse* (a few hundred non-zeros per document across tens of thousands of columns; sparse representation, cf. Refresher CS).
:::

::::: def
[Definition 2.2 — TF-IDF]{.tag}

::: key
[Key result — TF-IDF weight]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{tfidf}(t, d) = \mathrm{tf}(t, d) \times \underbrace{\log\frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)}}_{\mathrm{idf}(t)},
$$
:::

$\mathrm{tf}$ = frequency of the term in the document, $\mathrm{df}$ = number of documents containing the term, $n$ = number of documents. It penalizes omnipresent terms and rewards discriminative ones.

**L2 weighting**: we post-normalize $\tilde d = d / \|d\|_2$, so that *the dot product is directly the cosine similarity* — this is what `TfidfVectorizer` does by default.
:::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — IDF = pointwise mutual information]{.tag} Let us choose a document $D$ uniformly among the $n$, and let $T$ denote the event "$D$ contains the term $t$".

Then for any document $d$ containing $t$:
$$
\mathrm{PMI}(T\,;D=d) \;=\; \log\frac{\mathbb{P}(T,\,D=d)}{\mathbb{P}(T)\,\mathbb{P}(D=d)} \;=\; \log\frac{n}{\mathrm{df}(t)} \;=\; \mathrm{idf}(t).
$$

In other words: IDF is exactly the pointwise mutual information between "the event $t$ occurs" and the choice of this particular document. A term present everywhere identifies no document (zero PMI); a rare term strongly identifies the documents that contain it.

::: proof
$\mathbb{P}(D=d)=1/n$ and $\mathbb{P}(T)=\mathrm{df}(t)/n$, so $\mathbb{P}(T,D=d)=\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbf{1}[t\in d]$. Substituting:
$$
\mathrm{PMI} = \log\frac{\mathbf{1}[t\in d]/n}{(\mathrm{df}/n)(1/n)} = \log\frac{n\,\mathbf{1}[t\in d]}{\mathrm{df}},
$$
which equals $\mathrm{idf}(t)$ if $t \in d$ (and $-\infty$ otherwise). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Common variants (all useful in practice)]{.tag}

-   **Sublinear TF**: $1+\log \mathrm{tf}$ — "3 occurrences do not signal the topic 3× more than a single one";
-   **Boolean TF**: $\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{tf}>0]$ — robust to highly repetitive documents (spam, bots);
-   **Smoothed IDF**: $\log\frac{1+n}{1+\mathrm{df}}+1$ (the scikit-learn variant) — avoids blow-ups for $\mathrm{df}=n$;
-   **Composite schemes** (SMART nomenclature): different weighting on the document side (e.g. L2 of log-tf × idf) and on the query side (e.g. plain cosine); the performance of a search engine is often tuned here, before any model.
:::

:::: thm
[Model 2.4 — BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza) and its probabilistic reading]{.tag} A direct heir of probabilistic information retrieval (the Robertson–Sparck Jones 2-Poisson framework): a document is a mixture of "informative / non-informative" for the query.

The number of occurrences $x$ of the term follows a Poisson law of intensity $\mu_1$ in the documents that are really *about* the term ("elite" documents) and of intensity $\mu_0 \ll \mu_1$ in the others, and relevance is only correlated with eliteness.

The resulting weight of $x$ is the log-odds of relevance under this *mixture*: it is $0$ at $x = 0$, increasing, and *saturating* as $x$ grows (for a single pair of Poisson laws, the log-likelihood ratio $\;x\log\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_0}-(\mu_1-\mu_0)\;$ would grow linearly; it is the mixture that bounds it).

BM25 approximates this shape:

::: key
[Key result — the BM25 score]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{BM25}(q,d)=\sum_{t\in q}\mathrm{idf}_{25}(t)\cdot \frac{\mathrm{tf}(t,d)\,(k_1+1)}{\mathrm{tf}(t,d)+k_1\!\left(1-b+b\,\frac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)},\qquad \mathrm{idf}_{25}(t)=\log\frac{n-\mathrm{df}(t)+0.5}{\mathrm{df}(t)+0.5},
$$
:::

where $|d|$ is the length of $d$ in tokens, $\mathrm{avgdl}$ the average length over the corpus, and $k_1 \in [1.2, 2]$, $b = 0.75$ the usual defaults of the two tuning parameters.

::: proof
Two limits to know by heart.

-   **Saturation**: as $\mathrm{tf}\to\infty$, the factor tends to $k_1+1$ (bounded); at $\mathrm{tf}=0$ it equals $0$.
-   **Half-saturation**: it reaches half of its maximum when
    $$
    \mathrm{tf}=k_1(1-b+b|d|/\mathrm{avgdl})
    $$
    — $k_1$ tunes the saturation speed, $b$ the length penalty ($b=0$: no normalization; $b=1$: proportional).

These are exactly the two flaws of raw TF-IDF that BM25 corrects: unbounded linear growth on the tf side, and no handling of document length. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

|  | TF-IDF + cosine | BM25 | Set similarities | WMD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Formula | $\mathrm{tf}\cdot\mathrm{idf}$, normalized dot product | probabilistic weighting, saturating tf | Jaccard $\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}$ | transport distance between embeddings |
| What matters | weighted presence | presence *and* saturated density | set overlap | semantic alignment of words |
| Typical use | classification features (ch. 3) | search / retrieval (ch. 8, M2 ch. 7) | fast deduplication (ch. 8) | fine-grained similarity of short sentences |
| Cost | linear, sparse | linear, sparse | linear | linear program (Optimal Transport module) |

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.5 — Hashing trick for giant vocabularies]{.tag} For huge or *a priori unbounded* $|V|$ (tweet streams, logs): hash each term $h(t) \in \{1,\dots,D\}$ with a random sign $s(t)\in\{\pm1\}$, and set $\tilde x_i = \sum_{t:\,h(t)=i} s(t)\,x_t$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\,\langle \tilde x,\tilde y\rangle = \langle x,y\rangle
$$
— collisions cancel out *in expectation*.

::: proof
We have
$$
\tilde x^\top\tilde y = \sum_{t,t'} s(t)s(t')\,x_t y_{t'}\,\mathbf{1}[h(t)=h(t')]
$$
and $\mathbb{E}[s(t)s(t')]=\mathbf{1}[t=t']$ (independent signs); what remains is $\sum_t x_t y_t$.

The standard deviation of the collision term decreases like $1/\sqrt{D}$: with $D\sim 2^{20}$, the approximation is excellent for classification. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Geometry of documents]{.tag} Each document becomes a point in $\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$; we measure similarities (cosine), classify (Naive Bayes, SVM), cluster (k-means). The limitation of BoW: *bag* = no order and no semantics; "the cat eats the mouse" ≈ "the mouse eats the cat".

Embeddings (ch. 4) and transformers (ch. 7) answer this. BM25 remains *the* baseline of any retrieval system — including RAG (M2 LLMs, ch. 7, where it serves as a reference point for dense retrievers).
:::

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

corpus = ["graphe de connaissances entreprise",
          "réseau de neurones profond",
          "graphe neuronal et réseau d'entreprise"]
X = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(corpus)      # sparse matrix (3, |V|), L2-normalized
print(cosine_similarity(X).round(2))             # docs 0 and 2 are the closest

toks = [d.split() for d in corpus]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(toks)
print(bm25.get_scores("réseau entreprise".split()))  # BM25 score per document
```

### 2.1. Search engines: inverted index and ranking evaluation

Information retrieval, named first among the applications of the official description, needs two more ingredients than a scoring function: a data structure that avoids scoring every document, and a way to measure whether the ranking is good.

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Inverted index]{.tag} For each term $t$, the index stores a *posting list* of pairs $(\text{doc id}, \mathrm{tf}(t, d))$ sorted by document id, together with $\mathrm{df}(t)$ and the document lengths $|d|$.

A query $q$ reads only the posting lists of its own terms, at cost $\sum_{t \in q} \mathrm{df}(t)$ instead of $n\,|q|$; scores (TF-IDF, BM25) are accumulated per document and the top $k$ kept in a heap.

Because the BM25 term factor is bounded by $k_1 + 1$ (Model 2.4), each term has an upper bound on its contribution, and *dynamic pruning* (MaxScore, WAND) skips documents that cannot enter the current top $k$.

Posting lists store the *gaps* between consecutive ids with variable-length codes; by Zipf's law most terms are rare, so most lists are short.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.7 — Ranking evaluation]{.tag} For a query with $R$ relevant documents and a ranked list:

-   **Precision@k** $= \#\{\text{relevant in the top } k\}/k$;
-   **Recall@k** $= \#\{\text{relevant in the top } k\}/R$;
-   **average precision**
    $$
    \mathrm{AP} = \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k\,:\,\text{doc at rank } k \text{ relevant}} \mathrm{P@}k,
    $$
    and MAP its mean over queries;
-   **reciprocal rank** $1/\text{rank of the first relevant document}$ (MRR over queries).

With graded relevance $\mathrm{rel}_i$:
$$
\mathrm{DCG@}k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{2^{\mathrm{rel}_i} - 1}{\log_2(i + 1)}, \qquad \mathrm{nDCG@}k = \frac{\mathrm{DCG@}k}{\mathrm{IDCG@}k} \in [0, 1],
$$
where IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering. These are also the metrics of the retrievers of RAG systems (M2 LLMs, ch. 7) and of the recommenders of section 8.5.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — Evaluating one ranked list]{.tag} A collection has $R = 3$ relevant documents for a query, and the engine returns five documents judged (relevant, not, relevant, not, relevant).

-   Precision: $\mathrm{P@}1 = 1$, $\mathrm{P@}3 = 2/3$, $\mathrm{P@}5 = 3/5$.
-   Average precision:
    $$
    \mathrm{AP} = \frac13\big(1 + \frac23 + \frac35\big) \approx 0.756 ;
    $$
    the reciprocal rank is $1$.
-   With graded judgments $(3, 0, 2, 0, 1)$:
    $$
    \mathrm{DCG@}5 = \frac{7}{1} + \frac{3}{\log_2 4} + \frac{1}{\log_2 6} \approx 7 + 1.5 + 0.387 = 8.887 ;
    $$
-   the ideal order $(3, 2, 1, 0, 0)$ gives
    $$
    \mathrm{IDCG@}5 = 7 + \frac{3}{\log_2 3} + \frac{1}{2} \approx 9.393 .
    $$

So $\mathrm{nDCG@}5 \approx 0.946$.

Swapping the documents at ranks 2 and 3 would make the list ideal.
:::

## 3. Text classification {#ch3}

Deciding which category a document belongs to — spam or not, which team should handle a ticket, positive or negative review — is the most common NLP task in industry. This chapter builds the two reference classifiers on the bag-of-words vectors of ch. 2, Naive Bayes and regularized logistic regression, together with the evaluation practice that goes with them.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — Multinomial Naive Bayes, derived]{.tag} With the (false!) assumption of word independence given the class,
$$
\mathbb{P}(d\mid c)=\prod_{t\in d}\mathbb{P}(t\mid c)^{\mathrm{tf}(t,d)},
$$
and Bayes:
$$
\hat c = \arg\max_c \Big[\log \mathbb{P}(c) + \sum_{t\in d}\mathrm{tf}(t,d)\log \mathbb{P}(t\mid c)\Big].
$$

MLE of the parameters:
$$
\mathbb{P}(t\mid c)=\frac{n_{t,c}}{n_c},
$$
where $n_{t,c}$ is the number of occurrences of $t$ in the documents of class $c$ and $n_c = \sum_t n_{t,c}$, and
$$
\mathbb{P}(c)=\frac{N_c}{N}
$$
($N_c$ documents of class $c$ among $N$).

**Laplace smoothing**:
$$
\mathbb{P}(t\mid c)=\frac{n_{t,c}+1}{n_c+|V|}.
$$

::: proof
1.  The MLE comes from maximizing the multinomial log-likelihood under the constraint $\sum_t \mathbb{P}(t\mid c)=1$ (Lagrange multipliers — relative counts).
2.  Problem: a word seen at test time but never in class $c$ gives $\log 0 = -\infty$ — a single rare word wipes out the whole class, and on small corpora this happens constantly.
3.  Laplace smoothing is the *posterior mean* under a uniform Dirichlet$(1,\dots,1)$ prior: the posterior density
    $$
    \propto \prod_t \pi_t^{n_{t,c}}\cdot\prod_t\pi_t^{1-1}
    $$
    is that of a Dirichlet$(n_{1,c}+1, \dots, n_{|V|,c}+1)$, whose mean is $\frac{n_{t,c}+1}{n_c+|V|}$ (equivalently, it is the MAP under a Dirichlet$(2,\dots,2)$ prior) — the exact Bayesian link of ch. 0. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why NB works despite an absurd assumption]{.tag} Conditional independence is massively violated ("New" predicts "York"). But the *decision* (argmax) is often correct even when the *probabilities* are badly calibrated: it is enough for the right candidate to win, not for its score to be right (the theory of Domingos & Pazzani). Hence NB's status: bad probabilities, good baseline — always the *first* one in a text project, because it trains in seconds and sets the performance floor.
:::

::: prop
[Sparse logistic regression: why it works in high dimension]{.tag} On TF-IDF, $\#\text{features} \gg \#\text{docs}$ (10⁵ features for 10³ documents): the risk of overfitting seems maximal, yet the regularized linear model (L2, or L1 to select) generalizes very well. Three reasons:

1.  in high dimension the vectors are *almost orthogonal* — examples are naturally separable, and regularization suffices to pick a "sober" separator;
2.  IDF weighting has already done a large share of the statistical work (prop. 2.3);
3.  discriminative unigrams/bigrams are exactly the features a linear model weights well.

State of the art of the "classical" era until 2018 (Joulin et al., fastText); still formidable below 1,000 labeled examples.
:::

-   **Calibration**: when the probability is consumed (business thresholds, ticket routing), recalibrate — Platt (logistic regression on the scores) or isotonic; diagnostic: reliability curve (predicted vs observed reliability);
-   **Imbalanced classes**: class weighting (`class_weight="balanced"`), optimal threshold on the PR curve (not ROC); metric: **macro-F1** (per-class average — every class counts equally) rather than accuracy (which flatters the majority); per-intent confusion matrix for chatbots;
-   **Networks**: sentence CNNs (Kim, 2014) and BiLSTMs over the word embeddings of ch. 4; then transformer fine-tuning (ch. 7). Empirical learning curves: linear+TF-IDF wins below \~10²-10³ examples, the transformer above;
-   **Zero-shot / few-shot with an LLM**: zero labeled examples, k examples in the prompt (M2 LLMs): an excellent exploratory starting point and assisted labeling (active learning), rarely the final solution in production (cost, latency, confidentiality) — the trade-off is detailed in M2.

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_20newsgroups
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, classification_report

train = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="train", remove=("headers","footers","quotes"))
test  = fetch_20newsgroups(subset="test",  remove=("headers","footers","quotes"))

pipe = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(min_df=3, ngram_range=(1,2), sublinear_tf=True),
                     LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"))
pipe.fit(train.data, train.target)
pred = pipe.predict(test.data)
print("macro-F1:", f1_score(test.target, pred, average="macro"))
print(classification_report(test.target, pred, target_names=test.target_names[:3]))
```

## 4. Word embeddings {#ch4}

In a bag of words, "car" and "automobile" are as different as "car" and "banana": every word is its own orthogonal axis. Word embeddings replace these axes by dense vectors of a few hundred dimensions, learned from the contexts in which words appear, so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors.

::: thm
[word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013): distributional hypothesis]{.tag} "A word is characterized by the company it keeps" (Firth, 1957). **Skip-gram**: for each position $t$, maximize the log-likelihood of the context words $c$ within a window: $$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{t}\sum_{c\in \mathrm{window}(t)} \log p(w_c\mid w_t), \qquad p(w_c\mid w_t)=\frac{\exp(z_c^\top z_t)}{\sum_{v\in V}\exp(z_v^\top z_t)}$$ — a softmax over $|V|$ words at each position: $\mathcal{O}(|V|)$ per example, prohibitive. **CBOW**: symmetric (predict the word from the average of its context).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Negative sampling: the derived loss]{.tag} We draw $k$ "negatives"
$$
w_1,\dots,w_k \sim p_n(w)\propto \mathrm{freq}(w)^{3/4}
$$
(the unigram distribution raised to the power 3/4) and replace the softmax with a series of binary classifications "is this (target, word) pair a true context pair?": $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{neg}} = -\log\sigma(z_c^\top z_t) - \sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}_{w_i\sim p_n}\big[\log\sigma(-z_{w_i}^\top z_t)\big],$$ at a cost of $\mathcal{O}(k)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(|V|)$.

The gradient of this loss is derived in [Graph ML, Derivation 3.1](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch3) (session 4 of that course, the week before), the site's reference for it, where DeepWalk and node2vec reuse it on random walks. In short, the true context is *attracted* with a weight $1-\sigma$ that vanishes once it is well predicted, and each negative is *repelled* with weight $\sigma$, so a close but wrong word gets the largest correction. This chapter keeps what is specific to words: subsampling, the 3/4 exponent, GloVe and the shifted-PMI reading.

Theoretical interpretation: negative sampling is a form of NCE (noise contrastive estimation, Gutmann & Hyvärinen 2010; cf. Goldberg & Levy 2014).
:::

::: note
[Two settings that matter (and why)]{.tag}

-   **Frequency subsampling**: very frequent words ("the", "of") drown the signal; they are discarded with probability $p_{\mathrm{discard}}(w)=1-\sqrt{t/f(w)}$ (threshold $t\sim10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$) — the signal per pair stays intact and the computation is sped up;
-   **The 3/4 exponent**: flattening the frequencies boosts rare negatives, which are the most informative ones (frequent negatives are trivial to repel). The same exponent reappears in the weighting function of GloVe below: an empirical compromise between signal and coverage.
:::

::: thm
[GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014): least squares on cooccurrences]{.tag} Let $X_{ij}$ be the number of cooccurrences (words $i,j$) in the corpus. GloVe factorizes $\log X_{ij}$ with a *weighted* bilinear model:
$$
J=\sum_{i,j} f\!\left(X_{ij}\right)\big(z_i^\top \tilde z_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}\big)^2,\qquad f(x)=\min\!\Big[\big(x/x_{\max}\big)^{3/4},\,1\Big],
$$
where $f$ cuts the weight of rare cooccurrences (noisy, possibly zero; one cannot take $\log 0$) and saturates for frequent ones. The biases $b_i,\tilde b_j$ absorb the marginal frequencies.

Deep connection: skip-gram with negative sampling *is* an implicit factorization of a shifted PMI matrix (Levy & Goldberg, 2014) — GloVe does it explicitly, and globally (the whole matrix at once) rather than locally (sampled windows).
:::

::: def
[fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017): subwords]{.tag} A word = the sum of the vectors of its character $n$-grams (3 to 6): $z_w = \sum_{g\in G_w} z_g$. Consequences: an out-of-vocabulary word still receives a vector (the sum of its $n$-grams), and typos and rich morphology (German: compounds; French: conjugations) are absorbed. The same team shows that "fastText + bigrams" is a formidable classification baseline (cf. ch. 3).
:::

### 4.1. Evaluating embeddings

-   **Lexical similarity**: rate word pairs (SimLex-999, WordSim-353), correlate with the cosine — metric: Spearman correlation;
-   **Analogies**: precision@1 on $z_b - z_a + z_c \approx z_d$ excluding $\{a,b,c\}$ from the search (the Mikolov protocol): "king − man + woman ≈ queen". Caution: analogy accuracy is sensitive to word frequency;
-   **Downstream**: the real evaluation is the final task (ch. 3).

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — SIF sentence embeddings (Arora et al., TACL 2017)]{.tag} Sentence = weighted average with $a(w)=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+p(w)}$, where $p(w)$ is the relative frequency of $w$ in the corpus (an anti-frequency weight; $\alpha\sim10^{-3}$), *then* removal of the first principal component of the corpus:
$$
\bar v(S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{w\in S}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+p(w)}\,z_w,\qquad v(S) = \bar v(S) - u_1 u_1^\top \bar v(S),
$$
with $|S|$ the number of words of $S$ and $u_1$ the first singular vector of the matrix whose rows are the $\bar v(S)$ of all the sentences of the corpus.

::: proof
Why remove $u_1$: in the generative model of Arora et al., each sentence is emitted around a "discourse vector" $c_S$, but a common vector $c_0$ (syntax, function words) biases *all* the sentences of the corpus — that is exactly the direction of greatest variance, hence $u_1$.

The orthogonal projection removes this shared nuisance term; on Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), this single removal gains several correlation points and makes this baseline "simple but hard to beat" without a trained encoder. It is the direct ancestor of SBERT embeddings (ch. 7). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Bias in embeddings — the WEAT test (Caliskan et al., 2017)]{.tag} Two sets of target words $X,Y$ (e.g. professions) and two attributes $A,B$ (e.g. male/female first names). Association score
$$
s(w)=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{a\in A}\cos(z_w,z_a)-\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{b\in B}\cos(z_w,z_b);
$$
test statistic
$$
t = \frac{\mathrm{mean}_{x\in X}\,s(x)-\mathrm{mean}_{y\in Y}\,s(y)} {\mathrm{sd}_{w\in X\cup Y}\,s(w)},
$$
significance by permutations of the targets.

On GloVe/word2vec: scientific professions associate with the male attribute, artistic ones with the female — the corpus contains these stereotypes, and the geometry encodes them.

**Mitigation** (Bolukbasi et al., 2016): estimate the bias direction (PCA of the "he/she" pairs…), *neutralize* neutral words (remove their projection onto this direction) and *equalize* the pairs — we will see the "representation → bias → correction" pattern again in M2 (LLM safety, ch. 9 of the LLMs module).
:::

::: note
[Text ↔ graphs, the other LLGA bridge]{.tag} word2vec on *random walks* yields DeepWalk/node2vec (Graph ML module, ch. 3); conversely, a **Graph of Words** (nodes = words, edges = cooccurrence within a window) enables text mining with graph tools — this is a research axis of the course's professor, detailed in ch. 9: the words ↔ graphs loop is a signature of the master's program.
:::

```python
import gensim.downloader as api
wv = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")        # pretrained embeddings

def analogy(a, b, c):                            # a - b + c ≈ ?
    v = wv[a] - wv[b] + wv[c]
    return wv.most_similar(v, topn=3)
print(analogy("king", "man", "woman"))

# quick evaluation: do the neighbors share the context?
for w in ["graph", "court", "ticket"]:
    print(w, "->", [x for x, _ in wv.most_similar(w, topn=3)])
```

## 5. Topic models {#ch5}

A corpus of thousands of documents is too large to read, but it is usually about a few dozen themes. Topic models recover these themes without any labels: each topic is a probability distribution over words, and each document a mixture of topics.

::: thm
[Model 5.1 — LDA (Blei, Ng & Jordan, 2003): the full generative model]{.tag} For each document $d$ and each position $i$ of the corpus:
$$
\theta_d \sim \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha),\quad z_{d,i}\mid\theta_d \sim \theta_d,\quad \varphi_k\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\beta),\quad w_{d,i}\mid z_{d,i},\varphi \sim \varphi_{z_{d,i}}.
$$
A document is a mixture of $K$ topics; each word is drawn from the topic of its position.

The likelihood $p(\mathbf{w})$ sums over all assignments $z$ — intractable ($K^{\#\mathrm{words}}$ terms): hence the *variational Bayes* inference (original paper) or *Gibbs sampling* (practical usage).

Connected reminders: EM from the ML module (variational inference is its Bayesian version); Markov chains ([Reinforcement Learning ch. 0](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch0)) — the Gibbs sampler is a chain, recalled in the box below.
:::

::: recap
[Recap — the Dirichlet distribution and Gibbs sampling]{.tag}
**Dirichlet.** On the simplex of probability vectors $\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_K)$, the law $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$ with all $\alpha_k > 0$ has density
$$
p(\theta) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha)} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \theta_k^{\alpha_k - 1}, \qquad B(\alpha) = \frac{\prod_k \Gamma(\alpha_k)}{\Gamma\big(\sum_k \alpha_k\big)},
$$
and mean $\alpha_k / \sum_j \alpha_j$. It is conjugate to the multinomial: after counts $n = (n_1, \dots, n_K)$ the posterior is $\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha + n)$, and the next draw equals $k$ with probability
$$
\frac{n_k + \alpha_k}{\sum_j (n_j + \alpha_j)} ,
$$
which is the shape of both factors of Theorem 5.2.

**Gibbs sampling.** To sample a law $\pi(z_1, \dots, z_N)$ known up to a constant, resample one coordinate at a time from its full conditional $\pi(z_i \mid z_{-i})$, sweeping $i = 1, \dots, N$. With $z' = (z'_i, z_{-i})$, each update satisfies detailed balance,
$$
\pi(z)\,\pi(z'_i \mid z_{-i}) = \pi(z_{-i})\,\pi(z_i \mid z_{-i})\,\pi(z'_i \mid z_{-i}) = \pi(z')\,\pi(z_i \mid z_{-i}),
$$
so it leaves $\pi$ invariant, and so does a whole sweep. When every conditional is positive (here $\alpha, \beta > 0$), the chain on the finite set of assignments is irreducible and aperiodic, and the ergodic theorem ([Reinforcement Learning, Theorem 0.2](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html#ch0)) gives convergence to $\pi$.

**In practice**, discard a *burn-in* of a few hundred sweeps, watch the trace of $\log p(w, z)$ until it is flat, then average over well-separated samples, since successive ones are correlated.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Collapsed Gibbs sampling: the update equation]{.tag} By integrating out $\theta,\varphi$ (Dirichlet–multinomial conjugacy), the law of an assignment $z_i$ given everything else depends only on *counts*:

::: key
[Key result — collapsed Gibbs update for LDA]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{P}(z_i = k \mid z_{-i},\, w) \;\propto\; \underbrace{\frac{n_{k,w_i}^{-i}+\beta}{n_k^{-i}+|V|\beta}}_{\text{does topic \(k\) like word \(w_i\)?}}\;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{n_{d,k}^{-i}+\alpha}{n_d^{-i}+K\alpha}}_{\text{does document \(d\) like topic \(k\)?}}
$$
:::

where $n_{k,w}$ = number of times topic $k$ has emitted $w$, $n_{d,k}$ = topic $k$ in $d$.

The exponent $-i$ means "without the current position".

Each $z_i$ is sampled sequentially, over thousands of passes; the topics emerge by reinforcement (the rich-get-richer property of Dirichlets).

::: proof
By conjugacy, the marginal of the corpus factorizes into multivariate beta functions:
$$
p(w,z\mid\alpha,\beta)=\prod_k \frac{B(n_{k,\cdot}+\beta)}{B(\beta)} \prod_d \frac{B(n_{d,\cdot}+\alpha)}{B(\alpha)}.
$$

The conditional $\mathbb{P}(z_i=k\mid\cdot)$ is the ratio $p(w,z_i=k,z_{-i})/p(z_{-i},w_{-i})$: all the factors not touching position $i$ cancel out, by a property of beta ratios:
$$
\frac{B(u+e_k)}{B(u)}=\frac{u_k}{\sum_j u_j} .
$$
This leaves the product of the two predictive factors above. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Choosing the hyperparameters and K]{.tag} Small $\alpha$ = pure documents (few topics per document); small $\beta$ = pure topics (distinctive words). The *asymmetric* version (non-uniform $\alpha_k$) lets a "noise" topic emerge. $K$ is chosen by validation (held-out perplexity) *or* by coherence — see below; the two criteria do not rank models in the same order, an important result of text mining.
:::

::: def
[Evaluation 5.3 — Perplexity vs coherence]{.tag} **Perplexity** (held-out):
$$
\mathrm{PPL}=\exp\big(-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{test}}}\sum \log p(w_{\mathrm{test}})\big)
$$
with $p(w\mid d)=\sum_k \theta_{d,k}\varphi_{k,w}$ — but it correlates *poorly* with human judgment (Chang et al., 2009: models with lower perplexity may produce less interpretable topics).

**NPMI coherence**: for the $M$ most probable words of each topic, average
$$
\mathrm{NPMI}(u,v)=\frac{\log\dfrac{P(u,v)}{P(u)P(v)}}{-\log P(u,v)} \in [-1,1]
$$
over all pairs (probabilities estimated from document cooccurrences): it measures the actual collocation of the topic's words — well correlated with humans.

The engineer's rule: perplexity for predictive capacity, NPMI/$C_v$ for interpretability.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — LSA: truncated SVD as the PCA of text]{.tag} On the TF-IDF matrix $\mathbf{X}$:
$$
\mathbf{X}\approx\mathbf{U}_k\Sigma_k\mathbf{V}_k^\top ;
$$
the columns of $\mathbf{U}_k\Sigma_k$ = the documents' coordinates in the latent space (dimensions = directions of maximal variance, uncorrelated); $\mathbf{V}_k$ gives the topics (word distributions once renormalized).

Key differences: LSA is linear, deterministic, fast; LDA is generative, models the counts, yields interpretable mixtures — but LSA captures *weighted cooccurrence* and is often sufficient for document similarity.

Link with PCA: PCA = SVD of the centered-scaled matrix (ML module); LSA = SVD of the TF-IDF matrix (no centering: the "mean" of text makes no sense).
:::

-   **After LDA**: BERTopic (embeddings + clustering + c-TF-IDF) for topics on contemporary corpora — consistent with the "embeddings, ch. 4" pipeline; for the industrial use of topics: monitoring, compliance, e-discovery, detection of emerging themes;
-   **Word Sense Induction**: applying clustering to *all the occurrences of a single word* (BERT contexts) reveals its senses — the joint Vazirgiannis–Buscaldi paper of ch. 9 does exactly that, with mutual information maximization;
-   **Topic models on graphs** (TopSBM, Gerlach et al., 2018): the idea extended to networks (see the Graph ML module).

## 6. Sequences: NER, HMM, CRF {#ch6}

Some tasks need a label for every word rather than for the whole document: finding the names of persons and companies in a sentence, or the grammatical category of each word. Neighboring labels depend on each other (an entity that begins must continue), so this chapter uses models of the whole label sequence: hidden Markov models, then conditional random fields.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Sequence labeling]{.tag} Assign a label to each token: **POS** (grammatical category) or **NER** (named entities: PER, ORG, LOC…) in BIO ("**B**egin/**I**nside/**O**utside"): "*Kim*" = B-PER, "*Noel*" = I-PER. NER is the gateway to building knowledge graphs (entity + relation extraction, section 6.1).
:::

:::: thm
[HMM: forward, backward, Viterbi — the recurrences derived]{.tag} HMM: hidden states $z_t$ (labels), emissions $\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z_t)$, transitions $\mathbb{P}(z_t\mid z_{t-1})$. Notation: $\alpha_t(z)=\mathbb{P}(w_1,\dots,w_t,\,z_t=z)$ (**forward**) and $\beta_t(z)=\mathbb{P}(w_{t+1},\dots,w_T\mid z_t=z)$ (**backward**):
$$
\alpha_t(z)=\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z)\sum_{z'}\alpha_{t-1}(z')\,\mathbb{P}(z\mid z'), \qquad \beta_t(z)=\sum_{z'}\mathbb{P}(z'\mid z)\,\mathbb{P}(w_{t+1}\mid z')\,\beta_{t+1}(z').
$$

::: proof
-   **Forward**: condition on $z_{t-1}$.
    $$
    \alpha_t(z)=\sum_{z'}\mathbb{P}(w_{1:t},z_{t-1}=z',z_t=z) =\sum_{z'}\underbrace{\mathbb{P}(w_{1:t-1},z_{t-1}=z')}_{\alpha_{t-1}(z')} \,\mathbb{P}(z\mid z')\,\mathbb{P}(w_t\mid z)
    $$
    — by the Markov property, given $z_{t-1}$ the pair $(z_t, w_t)$ does not depend on the earlier observations.
-   **Backward**: symmetric, conditioning on $z_{t+1}$.

Uses: likelihood $\mathbb{P}(w_{1:T})=\sum_z \alpha_T(z)$; marginal posteriors
$$
\mathbb{P}(z_t\mid w)=\alpha_t(z)\beta_t(z)/\mathbb{P}(w)
$$
— this is the E-step of an EM to train the HMM (ML module). All in $\mathcal{O}(T K^2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Algorithm 6.2 — Viterbi: optimality by substructure]{.tag} The most likely label path satisfies the recursion
$$
\delta_t(z) = \max_{z'} \big[\delta_{t-1}(z')\, \mathbb{P}(z \mid z')\big]\ \mathbb{P}(w_t \mid z),\qquad \delta_1(z)=\mathbb{P}(z)\mathbb{P}(w_1\mid z),
$$
and the optimal labeling is read off by backtracking the argmaxes — $\mathcal{O}(T K^2)$ instead of $\mathcal{O}(K^T)$.

::: proof
Optimality: any optimal path arriving at $(t,z)$ has an optimal prefix up to $(t-1,z')$ — otherwise replacing the prefix with a better one increases the total probability (exchange argument: the future factors depend only on $z$, Markovian). So it suffices to follow the best predecessor: this is Bellman (RL module, ch. 2) on a Markov chain, with max instead of expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[CRF (Lafferty et al., 2001): the discriminative approach]{.tag} An HMM models $\mathbb{P}(w,z)$ *jointly* (generative); a CRF models $\mathbb{P}(z\mid w)$ directly:
$$
\mathbb{P}(z\mid w)=\frac{\exp\big(\sum_{t}\theta^\top f(z_{t-1},z_t,w,t)\big)}{Z(w)}, \qquad \nabla_\theta \log\mathbb{P}(z^\star\mid w) = F(z^\star, w)-\mathbb{E}_{p(z\mid w)}\big[F(z, w)\big]
$$
(with $z^\star$ the gold labeling and $F(z, w) = \sum_t f(z_{t-1}, z_t, w, t)$ the summed features) — *arbitrary* features over the whole sequence: word identity, suffixes, capitalization, shape of the neighbor, hyphen, position…, plus transition features $z_{t-1}\to z_t$ (which forbid O→I-PER: an entity start must be B).

Inference: forward-backward for $Z(w)$ and the feature expectation; Viterbi for prediction.

The gain over HMM: no "waste" in modeling the words, rich features, arbitrary interactions — long the state of the art for NER (CoNLL-2003).
:::

::: def
[BIO decoding and entity-level NER evaluation]{.tag} Per-token predictions must be converted into *spans*: an entity = a B-X (I-X)\* sequence. **Entity** evaluation (not token): an entity is correct iff both type *and* exact boundaries match; $$\mathrm{P}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{predicted}},\qquad \mathrm{R}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{gold}},\qquad F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}.$$ Token-level F1 (lenient about boundaries) always overestimates entity-level F1 — always report entity-level F1 (the conlleval standard). Industrial reflex: audit *boundary* errors ("Banque de France" truncated) separately from *type* errors (PER vs ORG).
:::

::: note
[Today]{.tag} Transformers label token by token (per-token softmax + BIO decoding; the head is often a *linear-chain CRF* or a simple softmax with BIO constraints in post-processing); the `spaCy` and `transformers` libraries (the `ner` pipeline) deliver the state of the art in a few lines; section 6.1 adds the relations, and the session-8 lab builds the entity-relation extractor that feeds the mini-GraphRAG of the Graph ML module (ch. 8 of this course places it in the full pipeline).
:::

```python
# Toy Viterbi: 2-state POS tagging (N noun, V verb), 4-word vocabulary
import numpy as np
W = ["le", "chat", "mange", "souris"]
p_z0  = np.array([.9, .1])                      # P(z1)
A     = np.array([[.8,.2],[.3,.7]])             # P(z_t | z_{t-1})  rows=prev
B     = np.array([[.6,.3,.02,.08],
                  [.0,.02,.9,.08]])             # P(w | z)  columns=words
seq   = [0,1,2,3]                               # "le chat mange souris"

delta = B[:, seq[0]] * p_z0                     # initialization
back  = []
for w in seq[1:]:
    m = delta[:, None] * A * B[:, w][None, :]   # (prev, cur)
    back.append(m.argmax(0)); delta = m.max(0)
z = [delta.argmax()]
for bp in reversed(back): z.append(bp[z[-1]])
print("labels:", [["N","V"][i] for i in reversed(z)])
```

### 6.1. From entities to relations {#relation-extraction}

NER finds the nodes of a knowledge graph; relation extraction finds its edges. Each extracted fact is stored as a row (head, relation, tail, source) — the (subject, relation, object, source passage) format that the GraphRAG pipeline of [Graph ML 10.1](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) ingests.

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Relation extraction]{.tag} Given a text $x$ and two entity mentions $e_1, e_2$ in it, predict a label $r \in \mathcal{R} \cup \{\varnothing\}$, where $\varnothing$ means "no relation".

Labels are *directed*: the relation from the first mention to the second and the one from the second to the first are two different predictions.

-   **Pipeline**: run NER, then classify every candidate pair of the sentence. It reuses the tagger of this chapter, but a missed entity is a missed triple, and the number of pairs grows like the square of the number of mentions.
-   **Joint**: one model predicts entities and relations together (table filling, or a sequence-to-sequence model that writes the triples). It shares evidence and avoids error propagation, at the price of a harder training.
:::

**Entity-marker classifier** (Baldini Soares et al., 2019). Insert markers around the two mentions, as in "[E1] alpha-methyldopa [/E1]", encode the sentence with BERT (ch. 7), concatenate the output vectors at the two opening markers and classify:
$$
p(r \mid x, e_1, e_2) = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W\,[\,h_{[E1]} ; h_{[E2]}\,] + b\big).
$$
The model is fine-tuned with cross-entropy, following Protocol 7.1.

**Distant supervision** (Mintz et al., 2009) labels for free every sentence that mentions a pair linked in an existing knowledge base. The labels are noisy: a sentence that names both entities often does not express the stored relation. Multi-instance learning ("at least one sentence of the bag expresses it") limits the damage, and the test set stays hand-labelled.

**LLM extraction** asks an instruction-tuned model for JSON that follows a schema, such as `{"head": str, "relation": one of R, "tail": str, "evidence": str}`, then *validates* every output. The JSON must parse, the relation must belong to $\mathcal{R}$, head and tail must occur verbatim in the source (this rejects invented entities), and both are linked to identifiers. Invalid outputs are retried or dropped, and counted.

**Evaluation.** A predicted triple is correct iff head, tail, label and direction all match the gold. Report micro-F1, pooling the counts of all relation types and never rewarding $\varnothing$. Benchmarks fix their own convention. SemEval-2010 Task 8 (10,717 sentences, 9 directed relations plus *Other*) ranks systems by the macro-F1 over the nine relations. BC5CDR (1,500 PubMed abstracts, 3,116 chemical-induced disease relations) scores the unique (chemical ID, disease ID) pairs of each abstract.

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — One BC5CDR abstract]{.tag} PubMed 227508 ("Naloxone reverses the antihypertensive effect of clonidine") contains the sentence "The hypotensive effect of 100 mg/kg alpha-methyldopa was also partially reversed by naloxone." Its candidate pairs are (alpha-methyldopa, hypotension) and (naloxone, hypotension). Only the first is a gold chemical-induced disease (CID) relation: naloxone *reverses* the effect.

Over the whole abstract, pairing every chemical and disease that share a sentence predicts 4 pairs, of which 1 is gold:
$$
P = \tfrac14, \qquad R = 1, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \frac14 \cdot 1}{\frac14 + 1} = 0.4 .
$$
The exported row is (MESH:D008750, CID, MESH:D007022, PMID 227508).
:::

The session-8 lab trains this pipeline on BC5CDR and exports its triples as (head, relation, tail, source) rows; the final mini-GraphRAG lab of Graph ML (session 12) loads them as its knowledge graph, and Exercise 14 measures each stage.

## 7. Transformers for NLP {#ch7}

The models of the previous chapters give each word one vector whatever its context, and read a sentence through a short window at best. Transformers compute for each token a representation that depends on the whole sentence; pretrained once on a large corpus, they are then adapted to each task with little labeled data. This chapter applies the architecture of the Deep Learning module to text.

::: recap
[Recap — the transformer block, for students who take Deep Learning in P2]{.tag}
**Attention.** From the token vectors $X$, form $Q = XW_Q$, $K = XW_K$, $V = XW_V$ and compute
$$
\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)\, V .
$$
If the $d_k$ coordinates of a query and a key are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance $d_k$. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ brings the logits back to unit variance, so the softmax does not saturate and its gradients do not vanish.

**Multi-head.** $h$ heads of width $d_k = d/h$ run in parallel on their own projections; their outputs are concatenated and mixed by $W_O$, for the cost of one full-width head.

**Masks.** An encoder (BERT) is *bidirectional*: every token attends to every other one. A decoder (GPT) is *causal*: the logits of keys $j > t$ are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so token $t$ only sees itself and the past.

**Block.** In the pre-LN form of GPT-2 and most recent models,
$$
h \leftarrow h + \mathrm{MHA}(\mathrm{LN}(h)), \qquad h \leftarrow h + \mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{LN}(h)),
$$
with a two-layer FFN of width $4d$. The identity path keeps deep stacks trainable; the original transformer and BERT normalize after the sum instead (*post-LN*).

**Positions.** Attention ignores word order, so positions are injected: sinusoidal or learned vectors (BERT), or rotations of $Q$ and $K$ (RoPE, M2 LLMs ch. 2).

Full treatment: [Deep Learning P1, ch. 6](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch6), or [Deep Learning P2, text generation with transformers](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-textgen); intuition: [Refresher Neural Nets, ch. 6](../m1p1-refresher-neural-nets/index.html#ch6). Here we *apply* the architecture to text; the M2 LLMs course (ch. 2) revisits it in depth (RoPE, GQA, MoE…).
:::

::: thm
[BERT (Devlin et al., 2019): MLM + NSP in detail]{.tag} Bidirectional encoder, pretrained on two tasks.

1.  **Masked LM**: 15 % of tokens drawn; among them 80 % replaced by `[MASK]`, 10 % by a random word, 10 % unchanged; the original token is predicted (output: per-position classification). The mixing avoids a pretraining/fine-tuning mismatch (the model will never see `[MASK]` downstream again) and forces a robust representation.
2.  **Next Sentence Prediction**: classify whether two sentences follow each other (the pair `[CLS]` A `[SEP]` B) — a weak task, abandoned by RoBERTa in favor of more data.

Result: `[CLS]` = sentence representation; one model, dozens of tasks via a simple head layer.
:::

::: thm
[GPT (Radford et al.) and T5 (Raffel et al., 2019)]{.tag} **GPT**: causal decoder — $\mathcal{L}=-\sum_t\log p(x_t\mid x_{<t})$, pretraining = predicting the next token; generative by construction, zero task-specific architecture (this is the family extended in M2).

**T5**: everything in text-to-text — span corruption (masking continuous fragments and regenerating them), every task (classification, translation, QA…) formulated as textual input→output; it unifies MLM and CLM.
:::

::: def
[Protocol 7.1 — Full fine-tuning (the stable recipe)]{.tag}

1.  **Head**: a linear layer $\mathrm{Linear}(d, K)$ on `[CLS]` (classification) or per position (NER, POS);
2.  **Optimizer**: AdamW, learning rate $\{2\times10^{-5}, 3\times10^{-5}, 5\times10^{-5}\}$ — a short grid, fine-tuning is sensitive but flat around the optimum; linear warmup for 10 % then linear decay;
3.  **Epochs**: 2 to 4 (beyond that: brutal overfitting on small corpora — watch the dev set); batch 16-32;
4.  **Small corpora (<1k)**: freeze the lower layers, layer-wise decay (*layer-wise lr decay*), or adapters/LoRA. LoRA freezes each pretrained matrix $W_0$ and trains only a low-rank update, $W_0 + BA$ with rank $r \ll d$ ([Deep Learning P1, Definition 7.1](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch7); reference box: [M2 LLMs, ch. 4](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch4)), so the added parameters are << 1 % — versioned adapters are revisited in the M2 ML Ops module, ch. 7;
5.  **Cost**: distillation (DistilBERT: 40 % fewer parameters, 60 % faster at inference, \~97 % of the performance of BERT), int8 quantization — the performance/cost trade-off is an engineering criterion, deepened in M2 (LLMs ch. 6, ML Ops).
:::

:::: thm
[Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019): the triplet loss derived]{.tag} To encode sentences in a comparable space (search, clustering, RAG): siamese BERT + pooling (mean), trained with a *triplet loss* on (anchor $a$, positive $p$, negative $n$):
$$
\mathcal{L}=\max\big(0,\ d(a,p)-d(a,n)+\varepsilon\big).
$$

::: proof
If the margin is respected ($d(a,p)+\varepsilon\le d(a,n)$), the loss is zero: nothing to learn. Otherwise, the gradient $\nabla = \nabla d(a,p)-\nabla d(a,n)$ *pulls* the anchor toward the positive and *pushes* it away from the negative; with this hinge loss, the size of the update does not depend on how much the margin is violated.

Crucial point: the quality depends on the negatives (mini-batch: the other pairs provide *hard* negatives — this is what shapes the space). This is the kind of embeddings that indexes the corpora of RAG systems — detailed in M2 LLMs ch. 7 (dense retrieval, reranking). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[French: CamemBERT, FlauBERT, JuriBERT]{.tag} CamemBERT (Martin et al., 2020): RoBERTa retrained on 138 GB of French text — the reference French model; FlauBERT: an academic French BERT; **JuriBERT** (Douka et al., 2021 — research from this course, ch. 9): an adaptation to *legal* French, where the vocabulary (doctrine, grievances, appeal) confuses general models. Multilingual: mBERT, XLM-R (100+ languages, shared embeddings — at the price of capacity diluted per language).
:::

```python
from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline("text-classification",
                      model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
print(classifier("Graph RAG is a game changer for enterprise search."))

ner = pipeline("ner", aggregation_strategy="simple")
print(ner("Michalis Vazirgiannis teaches at Ecole Polytechnique."))

# sentence embeddings for RAG (cf. ch. 8 and M2 LLMs ch. 7)
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
enc = SentenceTransformer("paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
print(enc.encode(["résumé automatique", "automatic summarization"]).shape)
```

## 8. Industrial text mining {#ch8}

This chapter assembles the building blocks of ch. 1-7 into *products*: summaries, keywords, deduplication, ticket classification — the real workloads of NLP in industry, together with their engineering pitfalls.

### 8.1. TextRank: extractive summarization by PageRank

:::: thm
[TextRank (Mihalcea & Tarau, 2004)]{.tag}

1.  Sentence → node; similarity between sentences $S_i,S_j$ (overlap of filtered words):
    $$
    w_{ij}=\frac{|\{t\in S_i\}\cap\{t\in S_j\}|}{\log|S_i|+\log|S_j|}
    $$
    ($|S_i|$ = number of words of $S_i$);
2.  symmetric weights → random walk;
3.  score:
    $$
    \mathrm{TR}(u)=\frac{1-d}{N}+d\sum_{v\to u}\frac{w_{vu}}{\sum_{v'}w_{vv'}}\,\mathrm{TR}(v),
    $$
    iterated from the uniform distribution (matrix power); geometric convergence to the unique stationary distribution (Perron–Frobenius: primitive stochastic matrix — a Markov chain reminder, ch. 0);
4.  the k top-scoring sentences = the summary (reordered chronologically).

The same algorithm on the graph of *words* (cooccurrence window) yields keyword extraction — "PageRank for text".

::: proof
The recursion reads
$$
\pi^{(k+1)}=\big[(1-d)\tfrac{\mathbb{1}}{N} +d\,M\big]\pi^{(k)}
$$
with $M$ the weighted transition matrix: the operator is contracting (factor $d<1$), hence geometric convergence at rate $d$ — typically settling in \~20-30 iterations for $d=0.85$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 8.2. Keyword extraction: RAKE, YAKE, KeyBERT

-   **RAKE** (Rose et al., 2010): split on stopwords/punctuation → candidate phrases; a word's score = $\deg(w)/\mathrm{freq}(w)$ (degree in the cooccurrence graph *within the candidates*) + bigram frequency; a phrase's score = the sum of its words. Fast, no external corpus, sensitive to stopwords;
-   **YAKE** (Campos et al., 2020): *unsupervised* statistical features per word — frequency, dispersion of positions (a keyword appears everywhere), case (a capital letter mid-sentence = signal), redundancy of variants (edit distance) — an aggregated score, with left/right windows for context; robust and multilingual;
-   **KeyBERT** (Grootendorst, 2020): extract candidates (n-grams), *embed* them (ch. 3), keep the ones closest to the document — and diversify with **MMR**:
    $$
    \mathrm{MMR}=\arg\max_{c\,\in\,C\setminus S}\ \Big[\lambda\cos(c,d)-(1-\lambda)\max_{s\in S}\cos(c,s)\Big],
    $$
    which adds to the set $S$ the candidate that is relevant *and* not very redundant; the same "embeddings + MMR" pattern returns in RAG (M2, ch. 7).

::: note
[Extractive vs abstractive]{.tag} Extractive (TextRank; BERT: ranking sentences): attributable, hallucination-free, but redundant and choppy. Abstractive (generating): fluent, but requires a generative model *and* a faithfulness evaluation — this is the territory of M2 (LLMs ch. 7-8) and of the M2 instructor's research (meeting summarization, cf. ch. 9). In industry: extractive remains the trusted solution when every sentence must be traceable to its source.
:::

### 8.3. Deduplication at scale: MinHash + LSH

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.1 — MinHash estimates the Jaccard similarity]{.tag} For uniform $h$,

::: key
[Key result — MinHash collision probability]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{P}\big(\min_{x\in A} h(x)=\min_{y\in B} h(y)\big) = J(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}.
$$
:::

Stacking $m$ hashings → a signature $\mathrm{sig}(A)\in\{0,\dots,2^{64}\}^m$, and the collision frequency estimates $J$.

::: proof
Let $z$ be the element of $A\cup B$ minimizing $h$ (a.s. unique for uniform $h$). Then $\min h(A)=\min h(B)$ iff $z\in A\cap B$.

Now $z$ is uniform over $A\cup B$ (permutation invariance of hashings), hence the probability $\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing): bands and rows]{.tag} The signature is split into $b$ bands of $r$ rows; two documents are *candidates* if an entire band coincides. Detection probability:
$$
\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{detect}}(J)=1-\big(1-J^{\,r}\big)^{b}
$$
— a steep sigmoid: with $r=5,\ b=20$: $J=0.5\to 47\,\%$, $J=0.8\to 99.96\,\%$.

The accepted/rejected boundary is "chosen" through $(r,b)$ — this is the exact deduplication mechanism used on LLM pretraining corpora (M2 LLMs, ch. 3, where it is detailed with scale figures; lab implementation: `datasketch`).
:::

### 8.4. Complete case: support ticket classification

::: ex
[Case study — 50,000 tickets, 40 categories, 3 languages]{.tag}

1.  **Data**: tickets (subject + body), heavily imbalanced categories (software \~30 %, licensing \~0.2 %); fragmentary annotation, noisy history;
2.  **Preprocessing**: NFKC (ch. 1), language detection, replacement of product references/numbers with generic tokens (`<REF>`, `<DATE>`) — *the highest-impact step*: tickets are 30 % codes;
3.  **Baseline**: TF-IDF (unigrams, sublinear) + weighted logistic regression → macro-F1 ≈ 0.72 — the bar to beat;
4.  **Model**: fine-tuned CamemBERT/multilingual (protocol 7.1) → macro-F1 ≈ 0.82; the main gain is on rare classes;
5.  **Errors**: confusion matrix — "login" vs "password" systematically confused (a fuzzy semantic boundary for humans too); solution: business-class merging or a rejection threshold (confidence < τ → human queue);
6.  **Production**: drift (new products → OOV): input distribution monitoring, quarterly retraining, active learning on rejected tickets (the most uncertain = the most informative).
:::

-   **Question answering and RAG**: retriever (BM25 — the direct descendant of ch. 2 — and/or dense; *hybrid search*) + generator; the reference module is M2 LLMs (ch. 7); the capstone lab builds a graph version of it;
-   **Monitoring**: stream → MinHash dedup → topic model (ch. 5) → keywords (8.2) → classification → alerts;
-   **French and multilingual**: corpora, multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R); legal/French = specific difficulties — JuriBERT (ch. 9) answers on the model side, Buscaldi's research (ch. 9) on the information retrieval side.

### 8.5. Recommendation systems

The official description names recommendation systems next to retrieval as a major industrial use. A recommender is a search engine without a query: it ranks items for a user, and text is one of its two sources of signal — the other being the behaviour of other users.

::: def
[Definition 8.2 — Content-based and collaborative recommendation]{.tag} Users $u$, items $i$, and a very sparse interaction matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{|U| \times |I|}$ (ratings, clicks, purchases).

**Content-based**: represent each item by a text vector $x_i$ (TF-IDF of ch. 2, or a sentence embedding of ch. 7), build the user profile
$$
p_u = \sum_{i \in I_u} r_{ui}\, x_i \big/ \sum_{i \in I_u} r_{ui}
$$
from the items the user liked, and score $\cos(p_u, x_i)$. It handles *new items* (their text exists before any click) but over-specializes.

**Collaborative filtering** ignores content and exploits the agreement between users: user-based neighbours predict
$$
\hat r_{ui} = \bar r_u + \frac{\sum_v \mathrm{sim}(u, v)(r_{vi} - \bar r_v)}{\sum_v |\mathrm{sim}(u, v)|}
$$
over the most similar users $v$ who rated $i$ (item-based neighbours are symmetric and more stable in practice).
:::

:::: thm
[Model 8.3 — Matrix factorization (Koren, Bell & Volinsky, 2009)]{.tag} Model $\hat r_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + p_u^\top q_i$ with latent factors $p_u, q_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$, and fit only the observed pairs $\Omega$:
$$
\min \sum_{(u,i) \in \Omega} \big(r_{ui} - \hat r_{ui}\big)^2 + \lambda\big(\|p_u\|^2 + \|q_i\|^2 + b_u^2 + b_i^2\big).
$$

**SGD update** for one observed pair, with error $e_{ui} = r_{ui} - \hat r_{ui}$:

::: key
[Key result — SGD step of matrix factorization]{.tag}
$$
p_u \leftarrow p_u + \eta\,(e_{ui}\, q_i - \lambda\, p_u), \qquad q_i \leftarrow q_i + \eta\,(e_{ui}\, p_u - \lambda\, q_i).
$$
:::

::: proof
The loss of one pair is $\ell = e_{ui}^2 + \lambda\|p_u\|^2 + \lambda\|q_i\|^2$ (biases treated the same way). Since $\partial \hat r_{ui}/\partial p_u = q_i$,
$$
\nabla_{p_u}\ell = -2\,e_{ui}\,q_i + 2\lambda\,p_u, \qquad \nabla_{q_i}\ell = -2\,e_{ui}\,p_u + 2\lambda\,q_i
$$
(symmetrically); a gradient step with the factor $2$ absorbed into $\eta$ gives the updates.

**ALS** alternative: with $Q$ fixed, the problem in $p_u$ is a ridge regression on the items rated by $u$, solved in closed form
$$
p_u = (Q_u^\top Q_u + \lambda I)^{-1} Q_u^\top r_u
$$
— independently and in parallel for all users, then the roles swap. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The model is the truncated SVD of LSA (ch. 5) adapted to a matrix with *missing* entries — a plain SVD would treat them as zeros. Implicit feedback (clicks) uses confidence weights on all entries (Hu, Koren & Volinsky, 2008).

**Hybrid** models tie the item factor to its text, $q_i = W x_i + \varepsilon_i$, which gives a factor to items nobody has interacted with yet; industrial *two-tower* retrievers push this further, with a user encoder and an item text encoder whose dot product is searched by approximate nearest neighbours.
::::

::: ex
[Example 8.4 — One SGD step, computed]{.tag} Setting:

-   $k = 2$, $\mu = 3.5$, $b_u = 0.2$, $b_i = -0.1$;
-   $p_u = (0.5, 0.1)$, $q_i = (0.4, 0.3)$;
-   an observed rating $r_{ui} = 5$, $\eta = 0.1$, $\lambda = 0.05$.

Prediction: $p_u^\top q_i = 0.23$, so $\hat r_{ui} = 3.83$ and $e_{ui} = 1.17$.

Updates (each using the old values):
$$
\begin{aligned}
p_u &\leftarrow (0.5, 0.1) + 0.1\,(0.443, 0.346) = (0.544, 0.135),\\
q_i &\leftarrow (0.4, 0.3) + 0.1\,(0.565, 0.102) = (0.457, 0.310),\\
b_u &\leftarrow 0.2 + 0.1\,(1.17 - 0.01) = 0.316,\\
b_i &\leftarrow -0.1 + 0.1\,(1.17 + 0.005) \approx 0.018.
\end{aligned}
$$

New prediction:
$$
3.5 + 0.316 + 0.018 + 0.290 \approx 4.12
$$
— the error went from $1.17$ to about $0.88$ in one step.

Recommenders are evaluated offline with the ranking metrics of Definition 2.7 (Recall@k, nDCG@k) on a *temporal* split, watching the popularity bias; the user–item graph view (PinSage) is in the Graph ML module.
:::

### 8.6. Web advertising and social media analysis

The other two industrial markets named by the description — web marketing/advertising and social network analysis — are text problems at their core: matching queries to ads, and reading short, noisy posts at scale.

::: def
[Definition 8.5 — Sponsored search and click-through-rate prediction]{.tag} For a search query $q$, the engine retrieves the ads whose advertiser keywords match $q$ — exact, phrase or *broad* match, the last one relying on query rewriting and embeddings (ch. 4, 7) — then ranks them by expected value
$$
\mathrm{bid} \times \hat p(\text{click} \mid q, \text{ad}, \text{context}).
$$

The click model is typically a logistic regression
$$
\hat p = \sigma(w^\top \phi(q, \text{ad}, \text{user}))
$$
over billions of sparse features — query terms, ad terms and their *crosses* — mapped by the hashing trick (Proposition 2.5) and trained online with L1 regularization (FTRL-Proximal, McMahan et al., 2013).

Because $\hat p$ multiplies a price, **calibration** (ch. 3) is a business requirement, not a refinement.

*Example*: ad A bids $2.0$ with $\hat p = 0.02$, ad B bids $1.2$ with $\hat p = 0.05$; expected values $0.04$ and $0.06$ — B is shown first despite the lower bid.
:::

::: def
[Definition 8.6 — Social media text and trend detection]{.tag} Posts are short, noisy and multilingual, full of hashtags, mentions, emojis and URLs. Normalization (ch. 1) replaces mentions and URLs by placeholders, splits hashtags (`#GenoaFlood` → "genoa flood") and keeps emojis as tokens, since they carry sentiment.

Typical tasks are sentiment and emotion classification (ch. 3, or a tweet-pretrained encoder, ch. 7), stance and rumour detection, and **event or trend detection**: for a term $t$ with counts $c_t(\tau)$ per time window, flag a *burst* when
$$
z = \big(c_t(\tau) - \bar c_t\big)/s_t
$$
exceeds a threshold, with $\bar c_t, s_t$ the mean and standard deviation over past windows (Poisson or Kleinberg burst models refine this for small counts).

Joining the text with the follower or retweet graph — communities, influence by PageRank — is social network analysis proper, developed in the Graph ML module; Buscaldi's flood-tweet study (ch. 9) is a research instance.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.7 — Detecting a burst]{.tag} A hashtag was used $12, 9, 11, 10, 8, 10$ times in the last six hours: mean $\bar c = 10$, sample variance $\frac{4 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 4 + 0}{5} = 2$, $s \approx 1.41$.

In the current hour it appears $31$ times:
$$
z = 21 / 1.41 \approx 14.8,
$$
far above a threshold of $3$ — a burst, which the monitoring pipeline then hands to keyword extraction (8.2) and classification to describe the event.
:::

::: ex
[Capstone project]{.tag} Full monitoring pipeline: corpus of 500 articles → cleaning/tokenization → TF-IDF + LDA (topics) → fine-tuned supervised classification → NER + relations (section 6.1) → export of (head, relation, tail, source) triples to the mini-GraphRAG (Graph ML module); evaluation at every stage (perplexity, coherence, macro-F1, NER F1).
:::

## 9. Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Buscaldi) {#ch9}

This module is backed by a laboratory (DaSciM, LIX, École Polytechnique — M. Vazirgiannis; LIPN, Sorbonne Paris Nord — D. Buscaldi): here is the *actual* research of the two instructors, each positioned with respect to the chapters of the course. A methodological lesson: every building block of the course (TF-IDF, clustering, graphs, embeddings) is a living *research argument*.

### 9.1. Michalis Vazirgiannis: text mining through graphs

-   **Graph-of-Word and TW-IDF** — F. Rousseau & M. Vazirgiannis, *Graph-of-word and TW-IDF: new approach to ad hoc IR*, CIKM 2013 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1145/2505515.2505671)); overview: *Graph of Words: Boosting Text Mining Tasks with Graphs*, WWW 2017 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1145/3041021.3055362)).

    **The idea**: represent each document as a graph of words (nodes = terms, edges = cooccurrence within a window), and replace the tf(t,d) of TF-IDF (ch. 2) with the *centrality* of the term — the sum of the weights of its edges (weighted degree). The weight captures the local cohesion of the term in the discourse, not just its frequency; TW-IDF improves ad hoc retrieval on reference collections.

    **Position:** directly extends ch. 2 — "counting becomes a graph score"; it is also the gateway to the Graph ML module (motifs, communities, k-cores).
-   **Keywords by degeneracy** — *Main Core Retention on Graph-of-Words for Single-Document Keyword Extraction*, ECIR 2015 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-16354-3_42)); Tixier, Malliaros & Vazirgiannis, *A Graph Degeneracy-based Approach to Keyword Extraction*, EMNLP 2016 ([aclanthology](https://aclanthology.org/D16-1191/)). k-core decomposition of the graph-of-words: the *main core* (the maximal subgraph in which every word cooccurs with at least k neighbors) isolates the words that carry the document — an *unsupervised, noise-robust* method that rivals supervised approaches.

    **Position:** the "graph" competitor of RAKE/YAKE in ch. 8; GoWvis demo (ACL 2016, [aclanthology](https://aclanthology.org/P16-4026/)); real-time version for conversations: EACL 2017 ([aclanthology](https://aclanthology.org/E17-2074/)).
-   **Clustering** — Giatsidis, Malliaros, Thilikos & Vazirgiannis, *CoreCluster: A Degeneracy Based Graph Clustering Framework*, AAAI 2014 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v28i1.8731)); Skianis, Rousseau & Vazirgiannis, *Regularizing Text Categorization with Clusters of Words*, EMNLP 2016 ([aclanthology](https://aclanthology.org/D16-1188/)): we *cluster the words* (communities of the cooccurrence graph) and classify the documents on these clusters — a regularization in small dimension, interpretable, that foreshadows the "topics" logic of ch. 5; **Position:** ch. 3 and ch. 5 (clustering in the service of classification).
-   **Word sense induction by neural clustering** — Abdine, Kamal Eddine, Buscaldi & Vazirgiannis, *Word Sense Induction with Hierarchical Clustering and Mutual Information Maximization*, AI Open 2023 ([arXiv:2210.05422](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.05422)) — *a paper co-signed by the two instructors of the module*: clustering the occurrences of a word by their *contextual* embeddings (BERT), with a mutual information criterion that is *maximized* — the exact dual of the "coherence" NPMI of ch. 5; **Position:** a merger of ch. 4 (embeddings) + ch. 5 (topics/clustering) + ch. 7 (BERT).
-   **JuriBERT** — Douka, Abdine, Vazirgiannis, El Hamdani & Restrepo Amariles, NLLP@EMNLP 2021 ([arXiv:2110.01485](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01485)): adapting the masked LM to legal French — cf. ch. 7; *it paves the way for Buscaldi's work in legal IR (below)*.

::: note
[Open extension: TF-IDF × LLMs]{.tag} The TF-IDF of ch. 2 selects the terms that identify a document; a current research question is to weight in the same way the *examples* shown to an LLM (in-context learning, M2) — the loop "classical weights in the service of modern models" starts from TW-IDF. A possible capstone project topic: comparing TF-IDF, graph-based TF-IDF (TW-IDF) and dense embeddings for ordering the examples of a prompt.
:::

### 9.2. Davide Buscaldi: QA, legal, sentiment, knowledge graphs

-   **Question answering by passage retrieval** — Gómez-Soriano, Buscaldi et al., *A Multilingual Question Answering System using an n-grams based Passage Retrieval Engine*, IICAI 2005, and journal version (*Answering questions with an n-gram based passage retrieval engine*, JIIS 2011): ranking *passages* by query-passage n-gram overlap (the direct ancestor of the BM25 scoring of ch. 2), evaluated in multilingual settings (CLEF QA) and on spoken questions (QAST). **Position:** ch. 2 (n-grams, retrieval) and ch. 8 (the retriever before RAG — the "R" of RAG in M2, ch. 7, has this history).
-   **Legal information retrieval** — Rosso, Correa & Buscaldi, *Passage retrieval in legal texts*, Journal of Logic and Algebraic Programming 2011 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jlap.2011.02.001)): retrieving the relevant passages in court decisions — long texts, technical vocabulary, cross-references: exactly the "legal French" difficulties of ch. 8, on the retrieval side (JuriBERT, above, handles them on the model side).
-   **Sentiment for crisis management** — Buscaldi & Hernandez-Farias, *Sentiment Analysis on Microblogs for Natural Disasters Management: a Study on the 2014 Genoa Floodings*, WWW Companion 2015 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1145/2740908.2741727)): classifying the emotion of tweets during a flood — classification (ch. 3) on short, noisy text, with subtle classes (worry vs alert); natural follow-up: troll detection (TexTrolls, [arXiv:1910.01340](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.01340)).
-   **Scientific knowledge graphs** — Dessì, Osborne, Reforgiato Recupero, Buscaldi et al., *AI-KG* (ISWC 2020) and *CS-KG* (ISWC 2022): NLP pipelines (entity extraction, relation extraction — ch. 6 and section 6.1) that turn millions of articles into a knowledge graph; **Position:** the exact outlet of the NER of ch. 6; these graphs feed the GraphRAG of the Graph ML module; the group's LLM-KG article series connects the module to M2.
