-   **In the LLM era: detection and memorization** — with Liyanage & Nazarenko, a benchmark for detecting generated academic text (LREC 2022, [arXiv:2202.02013](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.02013)); with Dentan, Shabou & Vanier: *Predicting memorization within fine-tuned Large Language Models* (ECAI 2025, [arXiv:2409.18858](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18858)) and the multilingual hallucination benchmark *MUCH* (LREC 2026, [arXiv:2511.17081](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17081)). **Position:** this research structures the "evaluation and safety" ch. 9 of the M2 LLMs module — the pedagogical continuity of the master's program.

::: note
[Common thread]{.tag} Vazirgiannis: *text as a graph* (ch. 2, 5, 8 → Graph ML, GraphRAG); Buscaldi: *finding information and making it reliable* (ch. 2, 3, 8 → RAG, M2 safety). Their joint paper (WSI) is the crossroads: contextual embeddings + clustering + mutual information — that is, ch. 4, 5 and 7 of this module.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ TF-IDF on paper.** On 3 given documents, compute by hand the TF-IDF matrix (natural log) of the reduced vocabulary, then the cosine similarity of each pair; verify with `TfidfVectorizer` (watch out for L2 normalization).

    ::: proof
    Solution (method):

    1.  count tf(t,d);
    2.  df(t) over the 3 documents, then $\mathrm{idf}=\log(3/\mathrm{df})$ (0 for a term present everywhere — it disappears);
    3.  multiply;
    4.  normalize each row $\tilde d=d/\|d\|_2$, so that $\cos(d_i,d_j)=\tilde d_i^\top \tilde d_j$ — this is what sklearn returns;
    5.  classic pitfall: sklearn uses the smoothed IDF $\log\frac{1+n}{1+\mathrm{df}}+1$; pass `smooth_idf=False` to recover the formula from the course. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **★ IDF = PMI.** Rederive proposition 2.3 in the cases $\mathrm{df}(t)=n$ (term everywhere) and $\mathrm{df}(t)=1$ (unique term); deduce why L2 weighting alone is not enough to squash omnipresent words.

    ::: proof
    Solution:

    -   $\mathrm{df}=n \Rightarrow \mathrm{idf}=\log 1=0$ — the term discriminates *no* document (zero PMI);
    -   $\mathrm{df}=1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{idf}=\log n$ — the term perfectly identifies its document.

    The L2 norm rescales documents, not columns: a frequent word keeps a high tf in *all* documents — only IDF (a per-column weight) squashes it. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **★ BPE.** Redo example 1.4 with the corpus `stage`×3, `stages`×2, `stand`×4 and list the 5 first merges; what happens if we add `stand`×40?

    ::: proof
    Solution (start): initial pairs (s,t)=9, (t,a)=9, (a,g)=5, (a,n)=4… — the initial (s,t)/(t,a) tie is broken arbitrarily; with `stand`×40, the pair (a,n) reaches 44 and *stand* becomes a token before the other roots — this is BPE's lesson: the vocabulary encodes *the corpus frequencies*, not linguistics. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **★ Analogies and bias.** With pretrained embeddings (GloVe fr), test 10 analogies and measure the success rate; compute the WEAT statistic on two sets of professions × two lists of first names; implement neutralization (projection removal) and measure the effect on both scores.
5.  **★ Viterbi.** Implement Viterbi for a toy POS tagger (2 labels, 5-word vocabulary); verify optimality against exhaustive enumeration; complexity $\mathcal{O}(TK^2)$; modify the proof of thm 6.2 for the case of paths with zero weights.
6.  **★ MinHash/LSH.** For $r=5, b=20$, plot $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{detect}}(J)=1-(1-J^r)^b$ and locate the "threshold"; which pair $(r,b)$ at $m=256$ gives a threshold close to $J=0.7$?

    ::: proof
    Solution: the sigmoid goes from \~0.1 to \~0.9 between $J\approx0.35$ and $J\approx0.65$ — threshold $\approx(1/b)^{1/r}\approx 0.55$.

    To target 0.7 one needs $b \approx 0.7^{-r}$ with $rb \le 256$.

    Then $r=9$, $b=25$ gives $(1/25)^{1/9}\approx 0.70$ with 225 of the 256 hashes (while $r=8$, $b=32$ uses all 256 but puts the threshold near 0.65).

    Keep the rule of thumb: threshold $\approx (1/b)^{1/r}$, and a larger $m$ makes the curve steeper. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
7.  **★★ BM25.** Show that the tf factor of BM25 is increasing, bounded by $k_1+1$, and reaches half its value at $\mathrm{tf}=k_1(1-b+b|d|/\mathrm{avgdl})$; comment on the effect of $b=0.9$ on a corpus of documents with widely varying lengths.

    ::: proof
    Solution: set $g(x)=\frac{x(k_1+1)}{x+c}$ with $c=k_1(1-b+b|d|/\mathrm{avgdl})>0$. Then
    $$
    g'(x)=\frac{c(k_1+1)}{(x+c)^2}>0, \qquad g\to k_1+1, \qquad g(x)=\frac{k_1+1}{2} \Leftrightarrow x=c .
    $$

    High $b$: long documents see their $c$ increase → slower saturation *and* a stronger penalty — suited when length signals richness; dangerous on heterogeneous mixtures of short/long documents. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
8.  **★★ Naive Bayes.** Derive the MLE estimator of $\mathbb{P}(t \mid c)$, show the problem of zero probabilities and justify Laplace smoothing as the posterior mean under Dirichlet(1,…,1) (theorem 3.1); implement and compare against `MultinomialNB` on 20 Newsgroups; test the effect of α on calibration.

    ::: proof
    Solution (core): Lagrangians → relative counts; a test word absent from the class → $\log 0$: the class is eliminated; the uniform prior adds a "pseudo-count" of 1 to every term → the smoothed formula; α>1 squashes differences (less overconfident), α<1 sharpens them (more discriminative, less calibrated). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
9.  **★★ Skip-gram.** Write the negative sampling loss
    $$
    \log \sigma(z_c^\top z_t) + \sum_{k}\mathbb{E}_{w_k \sim p_n}\log \sigma(-z_{w_k}^\top z_t);
    $$
    compute the gradient in $z_t$ and interpret it (who is attracted, who is repelled, with what force); implement on a small corpus and check that words with similar contexts have close embeddings.

    ::: proof
    Solution: gradient = $-\,(1-\sigma_c)\,z_c+\sum_k\sigma_k\,z_{w_k}$ (cf. Graph ML Derivation 3.1, with $z_t$ as the center); the positive is attracted with weight $(1-\sigma)$, the negatives repelled with weight $\sigma$; check: cosine neighborhood of "graphe" ≈ {réseau, nœud, arête}. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
10. **★★ LDA.** Write the joint law of model 5.1, integrate out $\theta_d$ and $\varphi_k$ and recover the Gibbs equation of theorem 5.2 in the case $K=2$, $\alpha=\beta=1$ (the multivariate betas reduce to generalized factorials); verify numerically the "rich-get-richer" reinforcement on 200 words.
11. **★★ Comparison.** On a classification task from your own corpus: Naive Bayes / TF-IDF+SVM / fine-tuned CamemBERT — plot accuracy vs training size (50, 200, 1000, all) and comment on the crossover.
12. **★★ Ranking metrics.** For a query with $R = 4$ relevant documents, an engine returns the ten-document list (rel, rel, not, rel, not, not, not, rel, not, not). Compute P@5, Recall@5, AP and the reciprocal rank; then, with graded judgments (2, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0), compute nDCG@5. Which single swap of two documents increases nDCG@5 the most?
13. **★★ Matrix factorization.** Implement Model 8.3 with SGD on the MovieLens-100k ratings (temporal split), with $k \in \{5, 20, 50\}$ and $\lambda \in \{0.01, 0.1\}$; report RMSE and Recall@10, compare with a content-based recommender on the movie descriptions (TF-IDF profiles, Definition 8.2), and measure both on movies with fewer than five training ratings.
14. **★★ Relation extraction on BC5CDR.** Use the training, development and test abstracts of BC5CDR (section 6.1).

    (a) Implement the sentence co-occurrence baseline and report micro-precision, recall and F1 on the test set, scoring the unique (chemical ID, disease ID) pairs of each abstract; check that you recover Example 6.4 on PubMed 227508.

    (b) Fine-tune the entity-marker classifier (Protocol 7.1) and report its micro-F1 with the gold entities, then with the entities of your NER tagger: the gap measures the error propagation of the pipeline.

    (c) Ask an open model of at most 8B parameters, in 4-bit, for JSON triples on 100 test abstracts; report its F1 and the share of outputs rejected by each validation check.

    (d) Export the triples of (b) as (head, relation, tail, source) rows for the Graph ML final lab.

    ::: proof
    Solution (method):

    1.  The baseline has high recall and low precision, since every co-mentioned pair is predicted ($P = 1/4$, $R = 1$ on PubMed 227508). Gold pairs never named in the same sentence are missed by every sentence-level method: their share bounds the recall of (b) and shows what a reader of whole abstracts, such as the LLM of (c), can gain.
    2.  Score (b) and (c) at the abstract level exactly as in (a), so that the three systems are comparable.
    3.  Count invalid JSON, labels outside the schema and entities absent from the text separately: each calls for a different fix (constrained decoding, a stricter prompt, span checking). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
15. **★★★ Capstone (project).** Carry out the project of ch. 8; each stage must report ITS metric (NPMI coherence for LDA, macro-F1 for classification, entity F1 for NER) and an error analysis on 10 examples.

The official assessment (SynapseS 2026–2027, as quoted in the fiche row "Assessment") is: "Not displayed: the 2026–2027 sheet gives no assessment modality, and its LLGA section shows no resit rule or pass threshold (those displayed belong to other programs)".
The scheme below is one possible design consistent with the session plan.
:::

### A classical assessment {#projects-exam}

With no published mode, this proposal uses the balanced default of these notes: a written exam on the in-class chapters, three lab reports from the small classes, and a group project that extends the capstone.

| Component | Weight | Format | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written exam | 40 % | 2 h, no documents except one handwritten A4 sheet, basic calculator | ch. 0–8 |
| Lab reports | 30 % | three notebooks, 10 % each: ranking metrics (Ex. 12), embeddings and WEAT (Ex. 4), NER + relation extraction (Ex. 14) | sessions 3, 5, 8 |
| Project | 30 % | groups of 3–4: the capstone (Ex. 15) or one card below; one-page proposal at session 6, report and 10-minute oral at session 12 | ch. 1–8 |

**Resit.** A 2 h written exam in the same format; it replaces the exam grade, while the lab and project grades are kept.

**Sample questions.** Five questions of 4 points each, 20 points in all, for the 2 h paper.

**Q1 (4 pts) — IDF and BM25 saturation.** (a) A document $D$ is drawn uniformly among the $n$ documents of a corpus, and $T$ is the event that $D$ contains the term $t$.

Show that, for a document $d$ containing $t$,
$$
\mathrm{PMI}(T\,;D=d) = \mathrm{idf}(t).
$$
(b) With $k_1 = 1.2$ and $b = 0.75$, compute the BM25 term factor of Model 2.4 for a term that occurs 3 times in a document of average length, then in a document twice as long. (c) What does each of the two parameters control?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) $\mathbb{P}(D=d) = 1/n$ and $\mathbb{P}(T) = \mathrm{df}(t)/n$; since $t \in d$, $\mathbb{P}(T, D=d) = 1/n$. The ratio is $n/\mathrm{df}(t)$, whose logarithm is the IDF (2 pts). Common error: treating the two events as independent.
- (b) With $c = k_1(1 - b + b\,|d|/\mathrm{avgdl})$, the factor is $3(k_1+1)/(3+c)$: $c = 1.2$ gives $6.6/4.2 \approx 1.571$, and $c = 2.1$ gives $6.6/5.1 \approx 1.294$ (1 pt).
- (c) $k_1$ sets how fast the factor saturates towards its bound $k_1 + 1$, reached halfway at $\mathrm{tf} = c$; $b$ sets the length penalty, from none ($b = 0$) to proportional ($b = 1$) (1 pt).
:::

**Q2 (4 pts) — Naive Bayes by hand.** The spam class has the training documents "win money now" and "win win prize"; the ham class has "meeting now" and "project meeting notes". Classify "win meeting now" with multinomial Naive Bayes (Theorem 3.1), (a) without smoothing, then (b) with Laplace smoothing. (c) How far would you trust the resulting probability?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- Set-up: $|V| = 7$, $n_{\mathrm{spam}} = 6$ and $n_{\mathrm{ham}} = 5$ word occurrences, priors $1/2$ each (1 pt).
- (a) $\mathbb{P}(\text{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = 0$ and $\mathbb{P}(\text{win} \mid \text{ham}) = 0$: both scores vanish and no decision is possible (1 pt).
- (b) The smoothed scores are
    $$
    \text{spam: } \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{4}{13} \cdot \tfrac{1}{13} \cdot \tfrac{2}{13} = \tfrac{4}{2197} \approx 1.82 \times 10^{-3}, \qquad \text{ham: } \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{1}{12} \cdot \tfrac{3}{12} \cdot \tfrac{2}{12} = \tfrac{1}{576} \approx 1.74 \times 10^{-3},
    $$
    so the document goes to spam, with posterior about $0.51$ (1 pt). Common error: denominators $n_c + 1$ instead of $n_c + |V|$.
- (c) The margin is a few percent and was created by the smoothing; Naive Bayes probabilities are poorly calibrated, so a business threshold needs Platt or isotonic recalibration (ch. 3) (1 pt).
:::

**Q3 (4 pts) — Viterbi on a two-state HMM.** The states are N (noun) and V (verb), the words "le", "chat", "mange", and
$$
\pi_0 = (0.9,\ 0.1), \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.02 \\ 0 & 0.02 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix},
$$
where the rows of $A$ are the previous state, and the rows of $B$ the state, with columns in the word order above. Find the most likely labelling of "le chat mange" and its probability (Algorithm 6.2).

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- Recursion stated, and $\delta_1 = (0.9 \times 0.6,\ 0.1 \times 0) = (0.54,\ 0)$ (1 pt).
- Second word (1 pt):
    $$
    \delta_2 = (0.54 \times 0.8 \times 0.3,\ 0.54 \times 0.2 \times 0.02) = (0.1296,\ 0.00216).
    $$
- Third word (1 pt):
    $$
    \delta_3(\mathrm{N}) = \max(0.10368,\ 0.000648) \times 0.02 = 0.0020736, \qquad \delta_3(\mathrm{V}) = \max(0.02592,\ 0.001512) \times 0.9 = 0.023328.
    $$
- Backtracking gives N, N, V, with probability $0.023328$ (1 pt). Common error: summing instead of maximising, which is the forward algorithm and gives $\mathbb{P}(w) \approx 0.0268$.
:::

**Q4 (4 pts) — MinHash and LSH.** Two documents have the shingle sets $A = \{a, b, c, d\}$ and $B = \{b, c, d, e, f\}$.

(a) Compute their Jaccard similarity and the probability that one MinHash agrees on them. (b) Signatures of 100 hashes are cut into $b = 25$ bands of $r = 4$ rows: compute the probability that the pair becomes a candidate, then the same probability for $J = 0.3$ and $J = 0.7$. (c) Is this setting suited to catching near-duplicates with $J \geq 0.7$ while comparing few pairs with $J \leq 0.3$?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) $J = 3/6 = 0.5$, which is also the collision probability of one MinHash (Proposition 8.1) (1 pt).
- (b) The detection probability is $1 - (1 - J^r)^b$. For $J = 0.5$ it is $1 - 0.9375^{25} \approx 0.80$ (1 pt); it is about 0.18 for $J = 0.3$ and 0.999 for $J = 0.7$ (1 pt).
- (c) Recall at $J \geq 0.7$ is excellent, but about 18 % of the pairs at $J = 0.3$ still become candidates, removed later by the exact Jaccard check at a cost. The threshold $(1/b)^{1/r} \approx 0.45$ moves up with more rows per band (1 pt). Common error: using $J^r$, the probability for a single band.
:::

**Q5 (4 pts) — Diagnosing a relation extractor.** In PubMed abstract 227508 of BC5CDR (Example 6.4), the gold standard holds one chemical-induced disease pair, (alpha-methyldopa, hypotension). The sentence co-occurrence baseline predicts 4 pairs; an entity-marker classifier predicts 2, (alpha-methyldopa, hypotension) and (clonidine, hypertension). (a) Compute the micro-precision, recall and F1 of both systems on this abstract. (b) Explain the classifier's false positive and propose two fixes. (c) An LLM returns the triple (naloxone, CID, hypotension) with a verbatim evidence sentence: which checks of section 6.1 accept it, and why is it still wrong?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- (a) Baseline: $P = 1/4$, $R = 1$, $F_1 = 0.4$; classifier: $P = 1/2$, $R = 1$, $F_1 = 2/3 \approx 0.67$ (2 pts).
- (b) Clonidine *lowers* blood pressure: the pair is co-mentioned in a treatment context, and CID covers only chemical-induced diseases. Fixes: hard negatives from treatment sentences, a separate "treats" label, or a decision threshold tuned on the development set (1 pt).
- (c) The schema, label and verbatim-span checks all pass, since both mentions occur in the sentence. Validation filters malformed and invented outputs, not wrong relations: "reversed by naloxone" is not "induced by", and only the comparison with gold labels catches it (1 pt).
:::

### Projects {#projects-list}

Every project uses public data, a laptop CPU or one free Colab T4, and only what this module, its prerequisites and, where a card says so, a mandatory course of the same period teach. Levels ★/★★/★★★ are those of the exercises, and the effort is given per student (★★ 15–25 h, ★★★ 25–35 h).

**Grading grid used by every project of this page** (a project card may replace one row).

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Question and success metric stated before the experiments | 10 % |
| Correct use of the course results (cited by number) | 25 % |
| Protocol: leakage-free split, baselines, at least 3 seeds, intervals | 25 % |
| Results and analysis: error analysis, limits, one responsible-AI remark | 20 % |
| Reproducibility: repository, README, pinned environment, one command | 10 % |
| Communication: report (≤ 6 pages solo, ≤ 10 group) or 10-minute oral | 10 % |

Group projects: a contribution statement and an oral with individual questions; the individual grade is the group grade times a factor in [0.8, 1.2].

#### P1 · ★★ · solo · Hybrid search on scientific and health corpora {#proj-1}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Compare BM25 (Model 2.4), a MiniLM bi-encoder (Sentence-BERT, ch. 7) and their reciprocal rank fusion on two BEIR collections, and report nDCG@10 and Recall@100 with bootstrap intervals over queries, against the BM25 baseline. |
| Data | [SciFact](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BeIR/scifact) — claims CC BY 4.0, abstracts ODC-By 1.0 (licence of the allenai/scifact release) — 5,183 abstracts, 300 test claims; [NFCorpus](https://www.cl.uni-heidelberg.de/statnlpgroup/nfcorpus/) — free for academic use — 3,633 medical documents, 323 test queries; loading: `load_dataset("BeIR/scifact", "corpus")`, with the judgments in `BeIR/scifact-qrels` |
| Chapters | [ch. 2](#ch2) (Model 2.4), section 2.1 (Definitions 2.6–2.7), [ch. 7](#ch7) (Sentence-BERT), section 8.4 (hybrid search) |
| Deliverables | notebook and 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 20 h per student · laptop CPU (encoding 9,000 abstracts with MiniLM takes minutes), longest run ≤ 30 min |
| Objectives served | O6 (health), O7 (retrieval engineering), O3 (the retriever of RAG) |
| Responsible AI | NFCorpus queries are health questions from the public: report the queries where every system fails, and never present the ranking as medical advice. |
| Going further | A cross-encoder reranker on the top 100, as in the dense retrieval of M2 LLMs ch. 7. |

#### P2 · ★★ · solo · Legal clause classification on a budget {#proj-2}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Classify contract provisions into 100 types with TF-IDF and logistic regression (ch. 3), then with a fine-tuned DistilBERT and its int8 version (Protocol 7.1), and report macro-F1 and the CPU cost per 1,000 documents, against the TF-IDF baseline. |
| Data | [LexGLUE, LEDGAR task](https://huggingface.co/datasets/coastalcph/lex_glue) — CC BY 4.0 — 80,000 provisions of contracts filed with the US SEC (60,000 / 10,000 / 10,000), 100 labels; loading: `load_dataset("coastalcph/lex_glue", "ledgar")` |
| Chapters | [ch. 3](#ch3) (Theorem 3.1, calibration, macro-F1), [ch. 7](#ch7) (Protocol 7.1, distillation and int8) |
| Deliverables | notebook and 4-page report |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 20 h per student · one free Colab T4 for the fine-tuning (≤ 90 min for two epochs at 256 tokens), laptop CPU for the cost measurements |
| Objectives served | O6 (public institutions, legal), O7 (cost-aware deployment) |
| Specific criterion | Replaces the "Results and analysis" row: per-class F1 on the 10 rarest classes, a reliability curve, and a rejection threshold that sends uncertain clauses to a human. |
| Going further | Zero-shot classification with an open model of at most 8B parameters in 4-bit (M2 LLMs), compared at equal cost. |

#### P3 · ★★ · group · Crisis monitoring on disaster tweets {#proj-3}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Extend the capstone ([Ex. 15](#ex)) into a monitoring pipeline: MinHash deduplication, an information-type classifier, LDA topics checked by NPMI, hourly burst detection and place NER. Report one metric per stage against its simplest baseline: duplicates found against exact matching, macro-F1 against Naive Bayes, NPMI against random word sets, and bursts matched to the event timeline. |
| Data | [HumAID, event-wise](https://huggingface.co/datasets/QCRI/HumAID-events) — CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — about 77,000 labelled tweets from 19 disasters (2016–2019), 10 information types; posting times are decoded from the tweet ids (milliseconds = `(id >> 22) + 1288834974657`); loading: `load_dataset("QCRI/HumAID-events", "hurricane_harvey_2017")` |
| Chapters | [ch. 1](#ch1), [ch. 3](#ch3), [ch. 5](#ch5), [ch. 6](#ch6), sections 8.3 (Proposition 8.1) and 8.6 (Definition 8.6, Example 8.7) |
| Deliverables | repository with one-command run, 8-page report, 10-minute oral with individual questions |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 20 h per student (groups of 3–4) · laptop CPU, optional T4 for a tweet encoder, longest run ≤ 1 h |
| Objectives served | O6 (social media, public institutions), O7 (pipeline engineering) |
| Responsible AI | Tweets are personal data: publish aggregates only, never texts with user handles, respect the non-commercial licence, and report the classifier's errors per event and country. |
| Going further | Drift across events: train on the 2016–2017 disasters and test on those of 2019. |

#### P4 · ★★★ · group · Biomedical NER and relations, exported to a knowledge graph {#proj-4}

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| Goal | Build the full chain of [section 6.1](#relation-extraction) on BC5CDR — chemical and disease NER, the entity-marker classifier and a validated LLM extractor — and report entity-level F1, relation micro-F1 against the co-occurrence baseline of Example 6.4, and the answer accuracy of the Graph ML mini-GraphRAG fed with the exported triples. |
| Data | [BC5CDR](https://huggingface.co/datasets/bigbio/bc5cdr) — public domain (NCBI notice) — 1,500 PubMed abstracts, 3,116 chemical-induced disease relations; loading: `hf_hub_download("bigbio/bc5cdr", "CDR_Data.zip", repo_type="dataset")` |
| Chapters | [ch. 6](#ch6) and [section 6.1](#relation-extraction), [ch. 7](#ch7) (Protocol 7.1), section 8.4 (RAG); the final lab of [Graph ML ch. 10](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10), mandatory in the same period (session 12) |
| Deliverables | repository with one-command run, 8-page report, 10-minute oral with individual questions |
| Effort and compute | ≈ 30 h per student (groups of 3–4) · one free Colab T4, open LLM of at most 8B parameters in 4-bit, longest run ≤ 2 h |
| Objectives served | O5 (LLM + graph), O6 (pharma, health), O3 (LLM extraction) |
| Specific criterion | Replaces the "Communication" row: the exported triples load unchanged into the Graph ML final-lab notebook, shown live at the oral. |
| Responsible AI | BC5CDR relations are chemical-*induced* diseases, i.e. reported adverse effects: an edge is an association stated in an abstract, not a therapy, and the graph must not be used for clinical advice. |
| Going further | Distant supervision from a curated database, and the pharma integrative project Y1-1 below. |

### End-of-year projects {#projects-capstone}

Seven of the eight Year-1 integrative projects use this module: relation extraction for drug repurposing ([Y1-1](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-1)), rumour classification and burst detection ([Y1-3](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-3)), text profiles for recommendation ([Y1-4](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-4)), time windows read from delivery notes ([Y1-5](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-5)), a sentence encoder for text-to-molecule search ([Y1-6](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-6)), finding extraction and report retrieval ([Y1-7](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-7)) and legal retrieval ([Y1-8](../m1-integrative-projects/index.html#y1-8)).

In Year 2, BM25, NER and the triple export of section 6.1 feed the transverse-project capstones [C1](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c1) (medical information), [C4](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c4) (retail assistant), [C7](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c7) (PII-safe assistant) and [C8](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c8) (public agency).
